A recent study suggesting that the muon's magnetic moment is anomalous could be resolved by a new scalar particle with negative charge. This new particle would likely have a mass around 100-300 times smaller than its decay limit, and could also explain why neutrinos are so light. If true, this would mean that any new particles discovered at the Large Hadron Collider would likely be the result of neutrino-related physics, rather than physics related to the magnetic moment. Furthermore, this discovery could also imply that the Large Hadron Collider needs a much more powerful engine to find these new particles. Additionally, building a device that can detect these new particles would require significant technological advancements, involving the development of a much more sensitive detector, one that can distinguish tiny changes in the behavior of muons when they are subject to strong magnetic fields. If constructed, this device could be used to study other fundamental questions in physics, such as whether time can be considered a fundamental aspect of the universe. It is anticipated that either a theory explaining the magnetic moment anomaly will be found in the near future, or the Large Hadron Collider will discover one of the underlying particles related to it, or find evidence that suggests these particles do not exist. A fundamental limit on the strength of a specific interaction in nature has been identified through the constraint that a major class of astronomical objects cannot collapse further. Specifically, this interaction, known as the "strong" or "fifth force," must be weaker than about 10^-12 times the strength of gravity. Researchers have now determined that the force can be no more significant than about 10^-13 times gravity. This study, based on the current understanding of white dwarfs, neutron stars, and black holes, establishes that the least massive of these compact objects has a minimum mass, approximately 0.91 times the mass of the sun. This finding has the intriguing consequence that if neutrinos have a total mass below a particular limit (approximately 8.6 electron volts) and consist of three distinct energy levels, the force would have to be stronger than about 0.2 times gravity, potentially making itself evident through a variation in the graviational wave signals associated with compact binary mergers. However, if the neutrinos have a total mass greater than this limit and only consist of two levels, the force could be as weak as desired. Furthermore, a more sensitive space-based experiment aimed at detecting the force is also considered, which would need a sensitivity improvement of about 10 times over present limits. A major aspect of this experiment would be the development of sophisticated simulations to accurately describe the interactions between the force and neutrinos within white dwarfs and neutron stars, which would involve a complicated linking of the effects on neutrino emission to the influence the force would have on the creation of heavy neutron stars and black holes from neutron stars. The study also explores an novel concept of "neutrinoless" mixed-mode oscillations, which could result in a distinctive variation in the spectra of neutrinos emitted from compact stars and could potentially be observed with a proposed generation of experiments focused on detecting high-energy neutrino spectra. The most prominent of these experiments, which involve detecting neutrino spectra from nucleon decay, have a built-in sensitivity to this interaction that is actually more stringent than the force's influence on the mass of compact stars. The implications of this research on the potential discovery of a "fifth force" in nature are twofold. Firstly, it highlights the need for a much higher sensitivity in experiments aimed at detecting this force, either through modifications to existing compact star research, such as studying neutron star mergers, or through the development of a dedicated force detection experiments, which would need a sensitivity improvement of about 10 times over present limits.

In recent years, Random Fourier Features have gained significant attention as a cost-effective method for dimension reduction in kernel methods such as Support Vector Machines and Neural Networks. However, research has shown that RFF can lead to diminished performance and reduced dimensionality in feature space. To address these limitations, we introduce Pseudo Random Fourier Features, an enhanced RFF technique that utilizes an optimal number of pseudo sources to generate features. The pseudo sources are derived from approximate eigenvectors of the kernel matrix through randomized techniques. The proposed method, PRRFF, results in a significant increase in feature dimensionality and enhanced prediction performance when compared to the conventional RFF method. The pseudo sources also enable the application of localized pseudo data, leading to adapted feature learning and enhanced prediction performance. The proposed method also facilitates efficient learning of neural network kernels and yields superior results when compared to state-of-the-art methods in various classification tasks. The method is accompanied by theoretical justifications and responsive experiments. The code is available at https://github.com/younesbablou/PRRFF.

This research investigates the Generalized Antenna-Switching Technique's (GNAST's) potential to enhance the energy efficiency of SWIPT-enabled networks. By incorporating an energy-harvesting base station, we analyze the maximum value of output power and the resulting energy consumption. To address computational complexity, the EAGF is adapted into more manageable forms: the Power-Based Formulation (PBF) and the Storage-Based Formulation (SBF). To verify our theoretical findings, simulations are conducted and shown to align with predicted outcomes. Enhancements offered by GNAST are confirmed to lead to significant gains in output power, efficiency, and time-saving at optimal solutions. Moreover, GNAST is demonstrated to offer greater benefits in scenarios with high output power and optimal solution computing times. Overall, our study showcases the GNAST's potential to effectively address energy allocation challenges in SWIPT-enabled networks. This model, though restricted to similar tail behaviors in both variables, identifies a key parameter that determines the tail distribution shape and establishes a statistical method for its estimation. This estimation method is based on maximum likelihood principles and utilizes the EM algorithm to find the best fit. Through simulation studies and empirical analysis, the proposed method demonstrates excellent performance in approximating the tail distribution, especially when the tail is heavily skewed. This method can be applied to any statistical model that includes a bivariate extension, such as the Pareto or Clayston-Copula models. Understanding language complexity is crucial for building efficient and user-friendly machine language systems. Researchers agree that to achieve this goal, they must develop a deep grasp of both the content and the syntax of language. Past research has examined the relationship between language difficulty and reading time, self-perceived difficulty, and machine learning models' performance. However, most of these studies only considered individual words in isolation, despite words often appearing in context that significantly affects their meaning. This study seeks to fill this gap by investigating the difficulty of words within their natural contexts. We first collected users' subjective difficulty ratings for words encountered in their daily reading habits and found that machine learning models struggle more with words in difficult contexts. We further analyzed the linguistic features responsible for this difficulty and found that both content and syntax play a significant role. We also discovered that words with difficult contexts tend to have different semantic properties and that context has a significant impact on the meaning of words. Based on these findings, we propose a new framework for understanding language difficulty, which involves both lexical and contextual components, and is influenced by both content and syntax. We further contend that future research in this field should prioritize the study of words within their natural contexts. We have made the data collected in this study publicly available in the hope that it will facilitate future research in this field. We have also integrated it into a new dataset that can be used to improve the accuracy of machine language systems when they encounter unfamiliar words in context. We have introduced a new evaluation metric that can determine how well a machine language system has grasped the meaning of words within their natural contexts. We have employed this metric to evaluate several machine language models and found that they struggle with words in difficult contexts, particularly when the difficulty is determined subjectively by users. We have also discovered that the best machine learning model under test conditions performs similarly to the worst one in difficult contexts, indicating a significant performance gap. We have proposed a novel approach that combines a machine learning model with a knowledge-based system to address this challenge. We have implemented and empirically evaluated this proposed approach, which significantly improves the machine language system's ability to understand words within their natural contexts. We have further analyzed the features responsible for this improvement and found that it is primarily due to the machine learning model's increased ability to understand words in difficult contexts. We have also discovered that the knowledge-based system's ability to understand words in difficult contexts is primarily influenced by its ability to grasp semantic features. We have conducted the main experiments under controlled conditions to validate the results and rule out the influence of other factors

Most current machine learning models that tackle sequential tasks like following instructions are based on language models that represent inputs as continuous vectors. These models primarily focus on processing individual input elements and their pairwise interactions. In contrast, our research aims to investigate whether machine learning models can effectively handle unordered instruction sets from various modalities ("draw a graphic like this picture, but with those words"). To tackle this challenge, we developed a novel approach that uses a type of mathematical structure known as a lattice to organize the instructions and incorporate their multilateral interactions. Our tests revealed that this approach not only rivals top-performing baseline models but also excels at sequencing instructions with complex relationships. Furthermore, our method surpasses human performance when instructions from different modalities need to be sequenced independently. Additionally, we discovered that our lattice-based model is particularly well-suited for handling diverse, unordered instruction sets from different modalities ("draw a graphic like this picture and that description"). In this scenario, our tests revealed that machine learning models still trail human performance. In summary, we believe our research represents a significant breakthrough in the area of sequential tasks and offer our code and data for public access.

Using Density Functional Theory and Dynamical Mean-Field Theory, we investigate the
spectral characteristics of SrMnO$_3$ with correlated orbitals considered.
Our study reveals that the observed spectral features within the energy range of
-5 eV to +10 eV are largely unaffected by the self-consistent dynamical
correlations. Nevertheless, using experiments and theoretical works, we show
that within the energy range of -5 eV to +10 eV, there are important spectral
structures that have not been thoroughly examined in prior research. For the
heavy Fermi liquid state, our analysis indicates that the intensity around
Mott-Hubbard gap is influenced by the hybridized 3d orbitals and that the
depth of this intensity is modulated by the atomic contributions from
neighboring 5d orbitals. Additionally, our research demonstrates that the
shape of the spectral distribution within the energy range of -5 eV to +10 eV
is determined by the spin and orbital correlations as well as interaction
strength at the Mn site. Our findings also include that upon increasing the
temperature from 300 K to 1000 K, the spectral structure undergoes
substantial changes and that these variations are more pronounced when the
electrons are not hybridized, whereas only minor changes occur when the
electrons are heavily hybridized, resembling an almost temperature-insensitive
heavy Fermi liquid state. Our studies provide a deeper comprehension of the
spectral characteristics in SrMnO$_3$ and highlight the importance of
including fundamental aspects of correlated orbitals in materials research.

This study examines the relationship between the frequency robustness of Molmer-Sorensen gates in ion lattices and the entanglement growth resulting from these interactions. We develop a theoretical framework that predicts how the durability of these interactions translates to resilience in entanglement and, ultimately, the transfer of an arbitrary state across the chain. Our findings suggest that a slight frequency adjustment can vastly improve the effectiveness of these interactions, allowing for a significant increase in the entanglement time or the ability to accurately mimic the behavior of monomers over a broader frequency range. However, our analysis also reveals that this improved performance comes at the cost of reduced scalability due to the increased need for precise frequency control. We propose a potential workaround to this limitation through the use of frequency-agile optical fields. We illustrate the potential of our approach through a simulation of quantum simulation of the Lindblad dynamics of the Hopfield model. This work has important implications for the development of large-scale quantum simulations using ion traps. It indicates that creating precise, scalable quantum simulations may be achievable not just for isolated monomers, but also for complex, entangled systems in these systems. Although this concept is applied to ion traps in this study, the underlying principles can be adapted to other systems based on two-level units. We believe that exploring these possibilities will have a significant impact on the field.

Investigating the effects of covalency and size of A and B cations within AB'O3 perovskites is crucial for understanding and predicting the structure and properties of these materials. To systematically analyze these effects, a set of pseudo-binary perovskites with varying volumes of A cation were created, spanning from small (K, Na) to large (Ca, Ba) cations. These pseudo-binaries allowed for separating the influences of A and B cations on the B-cation off-centering. Results show that both the equilibrium volume of the A cation and the B cation off-centering are intensified by increasing B cation size, yet in opposition to each other. Furthermore, B cation off-centering was found to be significantly affected by the A cation volume, but only to a minor extent when the A cation volume was small. These findings can be explained by a modified version of Glazer's rules and are supported by theoretical calculations using DFT methods. Additionally, the degree of B cation off-centering was found to be intensified by increasing volume of A cation in the series of Mn-based pseudo-binaries, but not in the series of Fe-based pseudo-binaries. This variation is attributed to the distinct differences in d-electron occupation between Mn and Fe. Consequently, this research offers a revised understanding of the structure of AB'O3 perovskites and highlights the complex interplay between A and B cations, necessitating a thorough examination of each system separately. Moreover, it underscores the significance of precise volume adjustments over subtle chemical substitutions. Finally, it emphasizes the value of pseudo-binary compounds as a means to investigate the effects of cation size within AB'O3 perovskites.

A novel bimodal beta distribution is introduced, distinctively addressing the limitation of previous data-generated distributions which solely rely on empirical data for parameter estimation. This new bimodal beta distribution is distinguished in its approach, where parameters are determined through a combination of empirical data and theoretical beta distribution properties. Specifically, the proposed model splits existing data into two parts, determining one parameter set empirically from each subset. This method is demonstrated on a real-world example involving the analysis of macroworld states across different microstates. A comparative analysis with alternative models reveals that the proposed bimodal beta distribution effectively captures the underlying structure of the data, as measured by the L1 norm, outperforming competing methods. Additionally, an investigation of the proposed model's scalability shows that bimodal beta distributions can be applied to a broad range of complex systems, including games, social networks, and lunar orbits. This new bimodal beta distribution provides a valuable tool for analyzing bimodal data distributions. The proposed method is available online as an open-source application.

The search for coldest dark matter, specifically heavy neutral leptons, can be deepened via existing and next-generation experiments that observe cosmic and terrestrial neutrino spectra. This investigation focuses on the implications of adding cut-free global neutrino data to existing limits from deep underground neutrino experiments, particularly LHCb, and forecasts future contributions from several prominent experiments, including: COMETA, LSND, and a proposed future long-baseline neutrino experiment at CERN. Existing analyses of LHCb data and cut-free global neutrino data reveal tightened 5σ confidence limits on the mass range of heavy neutral leptons, specifically: $< 0.8$ picoelectronvolts (peV) for massless sterile neutrinos and < 1.2 peV for massive sterile neutrinos with a mass up to 1 eV. Furthermore, inclusion of cut-free global neutrino data is found to significantly enhance the sensitivity of LHCB, LHCb+SHiP and combined LHCB and COMETA data by at least one order of magnitude. Additionally, even without adding global neutrino data, several experiments including LHCb, LHCb+SHiP and LHCb+COMETA expect improved 5σ confidence limits of less than 4 peV. When considering a 4 peV mass scale, the most sensitive experiments to implement this discovery scenario would be LHCb, LHCB+SHiP and LHCB+COMETA, all with sensitivity values of 1.5. Meanwhile, inclusion of cut-free global neutrino data is projected to enhance the sensitivity by at least one order of magnitude, with estimated sensitivity values of 0.1 for all three of these experiments. Consequently, existing and next-generation neutrino experiments have significant potential to substantially improve detection limits for heavy neutral leptons. Although deeply underground and long-baseline neutrino experiments hold prominent positions in this ranking, a notable role is also seen for COMETA, LSND, and CERN's proposed long-baseline neutrino experiment, all of which are expected to play important parts in the search for heavy neutral leptons. Moreover, this study highlights the importance of gaining access to cut-free global neutrino data, which would greatly improve the effectiveness of these experiments in finding coldest dark matter. The community should prioritize providing raw data for reanalysis in order to realize the full potential of these experiments in this coldest dark matter search. In a Sagnac interferometer, counter-propagating laser beams exhibit opposite Doppler shifts in opposite directions. This unique phenomenon causes a difference in optical path lengths, resulting in a phase shift between the beams. If the counter-propagating beams have unequal intensities, this difference in optical path lengths leads to a variation in absorption between the beams, potentially inducing a thermal expansion difference in the interferometer arms. Although the thermal expansion effect is typically considered negligible, it may, however, become significant under specific conditions, namely when the counter-propagating beams have vastly unequal intensities and there is a substantial intensity difference in the arms. Moreover, this thermal expansion effect can also arise with high-power lasers with small beam sizes, even without the need for counter-propagating light. Interestingly, this thermal expansion phenomenon can be utilized to develop highly sensitive strain gauges capable of detecting tiny changes in length, roughly on the order of 10^(-9). Furthermore, we propose incorporating a refractive index modulator into the Sagnac interferometer set-up, allowing for a substantial change in optical path length in response to a thermal expansion difference, and providing a strain gauge with improved sensitivity, potentially exceeding 10^(-7) strain per unit voltage. A theoretical analysis and practical considerations for optimizing the performance of these proposed gauges are also presented. A demonstration of a sensitive strain gauge, involving the incorporation of a laser with unequal counter-propagating light into a Sagnac interferometer, demonstrates the effectiveness of this method, showing a maximum sensitivity of approximately 0.53 Hz/ε, along with an experimental investigation of the strain gauge's performance. The developed gauge has an exceptionally high sensitivity in comparison to conventional mechanical strain gauges, offering implications for various sensitive optical metrology applications. Furthermore, this proposed technique has the added benefit of being able to measure strain simultaneously with interferometric accuracy, potentially allowing for error-free calibration of any mechanical device equipped with a built-in strain gauge. Lastly, possible extensions to extend the gauge's capabilities to measure other physical parameters, such as temperature or refractive index, are also outlined. The described technique is not limited to Sagnac interferometers, and potential applications in precision measurement of physical parameters are also explored. The technique is not limited to Sagnac interferometers, and possible extensions to temperature or refractive index measurements are also considered. The described method may also enable simultaneous measurement of strain and other parameters, such as temperature or the device's refractive index, potentially enabling precision calibration of mechanical systems.

We challenge a conjecture made in 2007 by Finkelberg, Koseleeff, Pyhra, and Siebert. This task involves understanding nilpotent fibres of a rational map between varieties defined over complex numbers. We prove that it's possible for a nilpotent fibre to include a dense orbit belonging to a specific subgroup, which is equivalent to showing that it's possible for an algebraic group to contain a dense orbit within a nilpotent subset. A single face image can generate a range of faces from the same individual based solely on the view, known as the equvalence problem. This issue must be addressed before the goal of building a face from an image and a sketch can be achieved. Previous research has suggested that views are represented by a low-dimensional parameter space with manifold structure. In contrast, our proposed model, called the Self-aligned Dual face Regression Network (SADRNet), instead posits that factors are organized in a high-dimensional space without a underlying structure and can be structured as a sphere. Specifically, SADRNet is designed to remove the equivalence problem by conducting a factor analysis of a face from an arbitrary view. For this purpose, our model consists of two learned sub-networks: one for decomposing a face from any view (source network), and the other for reassembling the face based on the learned factors (target network). The two sub-networks share the same structure but are trained from different factors. Since the target network is trained with faces having the same structure but diverse views, it can be used to eliminate the equivalence problem. In addition, our model includes a unique algebraic technique to reassemble faces from factors learned by the source network. For this purpose, the factors were learned using a novel approach based on the spherical structure assumption. Our experiments validated the effectiveness of our approach by achieving the best results in the face modulation task and face sketching applications. We investigate the electronic properties of a lattice with both spatial and temporal symmetries, specifically within the U(1) symmetric domain-winding construction. Our analysis focuses on the impact of a finite charge density on the fracton model, revealing a novel phase characterized by both supersymmetry and discrete lattice translation symmetries. This phase exhibits hierarchical mobility for the fractons, constrained to move along particular paths, as well as the ability to create and destroy charges at distinct rates. We find that lattice vibrations can transfer momentum to fractons with smaller hopping lengths, thus affecting their mobility. Furthermore, we establish the existence of a finite charge density that may impede the mobility of inner fractons, and this effect is nuanced in that it depends on the specific symmetry of the inner fracton. We also discuss the connections between our findings and other theories, including the dynamics of higher-form magnetic monopoles and the model of dual superfluidity. Lastly, we propose that this fracton phase may be relevant to the physics of certain systems involving strong Rydberg interactions and hierarchical algebras associated with spin and symmetry.

We introduce a novel framework for analyzing high-dimensional linear models that incorporate infinite-dimensional data. Our framework is an expansion of the well-known Generalized Linear Model (GLM) and is suitable for modeling scenarios involving time-dependent variables. We demonstrate that by applying a regularized least-squares estimator with an L1 penalty, we can obtain an accurate and efficient estimate of the model parameters. Our study establishes an explicit bound for the spectral norm of the operator mapping the parameter to the estimated variable, which provides a guarantee for the consistency of the estimator. Furthermore, we develop a practical algorithm for modeling infinite-dimensional data by employing a block-coordinate descent method. Our algorithm facilitates the inclusion of non-smooth penalties, such as the L1 penalty, and ensures that the estimate meets the desired quality standards. We also establish an explicit rate of convergence for the algorithm. Our method can be applied to a range of applications, including signal processing, neural networks, and dynamic systems. We showcase the effectiveness of our approach through numerical experiments in these contexts. We also investigate the method's scalability by applying it to large-scale synthetic data. Our framework is highly flexible and allows for the inclusion of modeling constraints, such as constraints on the matrix inverse. Our study is an initial exploration of the GLM, and there are numerous potential directions for enhancing and broadening the method. Our code is openly available online.

In x-ray free-electron lasers, the interaction between an intense, short x-ray pulse and core-excited states of a target leads to coherent electron motion in these states. This motion results from the sudden disruption of the excited-state distribution by the x-ray pulse. The motion of these electrons, however, is very rapid, lasting only a few femtoseconds, which makes it challenging to study. Furthermore, the effect of varying the photon energy of an x-ray pulse on the motion of these electrons is complex and difficult to predict. It involves a combination of influences, including the specific core level from which an electron is ejected, the energy of the excited state, and the presence of other available energy levels. In our research, we investigated this complex phenomenon by using an atomic hydrogen model, which enables the simulation of the coherent electron motion caused by an x-ray pulse of any energy. Our study is significant because it is the first to demonstrate the role of resonant intermediate states in core-excited systems and the associated electron dynamics. Additionally, our findings illustrate the potential of x-ray free-electron lasers to manipulate core-excited states and modify the outcomes of subsequent chemical reactions. Our study offers new insights into the behavior of Martian baroclinic storms, which are influenced by the planet's thin atmosphere. By utilizing a simplified model that accounts for both atmospheric density and the effects of solar radiation on temperature, we simulated atmospheric circulation under conditions similar to those found on Mars in the late 20th century. Our findings reveal that the planet's atmospheric circulation patterns resemble those on Earth, with permanent storms forming near the poles and mid-latitudes, shaped by the Martian surface's topographic features. These storms share similarities with those on Mars, and are fueled by the discrepancy between the temperatures at the poles and mid-latitudes. They also follow the Rossby wave theory, and our model predicts that an increase in carbon dioxide atmospheric density will lead to more pronounced storms, and suggests that the retreat of thawed CO2 polar caps during the Martian summer may disrupt the atmosphere's circulation patterns. Furthermore, our study predicts that the addition of water vapor to the Martian atmosphere will lead to a breakdown in circulation, and that this effect may be mitigated by increased solar absorption, but only if the atmosphere's density remains below a certain threshold. This threshold, however, is uncertain, and our study suggests that even a small amount of water vapor in the Martian atmosphere could cause a significant increase in atmospheric circulation and storm activity. This, in turn, could result in a breakdown of the planet's atmospheric circulation, and potentially lead to a return to the seasonal polar cap behavior observed in the Curiosity rover's findings. Ultimately, our study suggests that water vapor may play a crucial role in the Martian atmosphere's circulation, and that even a relatively small amount could have a significant impact. This, however, is subject to further investigation, and our study predicts that even a modest increase in solar absorption, where the atmosphere's density remains below a certain threshold, may mitigate this effect. The implications of these findings for the Martian atmosphere, and the potential for circulation and storm activity driven by water vapor, are far-reaching, and underscore the importance of continuing to study the planet's atmosphere through both modeling and observation. Most active learning algorithms in computer vision rely on theoretical models and are tested on relatively small datasets, such as Stanford 64 or CIFAR-10, but they fail to scale to larger, more practical datasets like ImageNet. This study aims to address this gap by evaluating and improving the performance of active learning on large, natural image datasets. We analyze various query strategies and find that straightforward modifications to top-performing batch selection methods can significantly improve performance on larger datasets. Specifically, using an ensemble of strategies and selecting a fixed amount of data for each iteration results in better results compared to choosing data in batches. We further investigate combining pool-based active learning with weak supervision, introducing the Simple Subset Selection algorithm, which shows excellent performance on large datasets while requiring minimal adjustments to existing strong baseline models. This method's performance surpasses existing strong baselines on the small dataset (around 200 images) and matches or exceeds their performance on larger datasets (around 5000 images). This study introduces Hamiltonian Neural Networks, a novel type of model that represents physical systems using graph-structured data. We demonstrate that HNNs can be an effective alternative to LSTM-based meta-learners in modeling physical systems and underlying dynamics. Our evaluation shows that an HNN achieves similar performance to an LSTM-based model in a few-shot learning setting on the rotoseg dataset, significantly outperforms it on the MNIST dataset, and successfully predicts complex dynamics in a curved wire scenario. Additionally, we find that training HNNs to optimize physical constraints such as energy minimization yields models that closely mimic actual dynamics, even when subjected to external forces. In contrast, our results indicate that LSTM-based models may be influenced by these forces and diverge from the actual dynamics. These findings suggest that graph-structured models like HNNs can efficiently capture the underlying dynamics of physical systems from sampled data. We have made our implementation and data available at https://github.com/google-research/google-research/tree/master/hamiltonian_neural_networks. We have also included an example of a hamiltonian neural network in the hamiltonian_neural_networks.zip file. Please see the README file for more information. Despite the promising performance of HNNs, there are several areas where further research is needed. One potential area of study involves expanding the class of integrable systems that can be efficiently learned from HNNs. Additionally, we have limited insights into the representation learned by HNNs, and further work is required to gain a deeper understanding of the graph structure and underlying dynamics being captured by these models. Finally, we have primarily focused on applying HNNs to systems described by ordinary differential equations and believe that they have significant potential for use in partial differential equations. We intend to explore this in future work. We hope that our study will spark greater interest in the development and broadening of applications for graph-structured neural network models like HNNs. We look forward to seeing the innovations that result from further exploration of these concepts. Airports require high-security standards to prevent threats like terrorism and illegal trade.  Image-based technology can enhance the security process by identifying prohibited items on individuals or in luggage.  However, existing datasets for this task are limited,  which hinders the development of efficient detection methods.  In response,  we introduce HiXray,  a new dataset featuring X-ray images of prohibited items,  including a diverse range of 19 categories from the US Transportation Security Administration's prohibited items list.  HiXray comprises 1,288 training images and 1,333 testing images,  compiled from various sources including real-world scanning images.  Our evaluation shows that models performance varies significantly depending on the dataset used,  with HiXray-based models outperforming those trained on other datasets.  Notably,  our research indicates that multi-task learning can improve results,  and provides methodology for adapting existing detection models to HiXray,  as well as source code and further analysis at https://github.com/ghulam-eisenstein/HiXray. Deep learning models in Natural Language Processing (NLP) have achieved great success in recent years. Improving their performance with large datasets is now a common practice, however, these models can also suffer from degradation due to overfitting and limited generalizability. In this research, we focus on enhancing the performance of these models using data augmentation techniques, which can generate useful new data based on labeled sets. Although applied successfully in other NLP tasks such as sentence transformations and text generation, there is a lack of comprehensive studies on data augmentation. In this paper, we explore different data augmentation techniques including word dropout, substitution, and rearrangement along with application of EDA techniques to create new datasets from labeled sets. We conducted comprehensive experiments on a range of NLP tasks including text classification, sentiment analysis and part-of-speech tagging from the GLUE and CoNLL-2003 datasets respectively. Our study shows significant improvements in model performance with data augmentation, averaging a 2.5% increase in accuracy across all experiments. Additionally, our findings reveal that word-level augmentations are more effective than character-level and sentence-level augmentations, and also, models with data augmentation perform better than distributed training with multiple GPUs. Our code and model predictions are available online for further validation and interpretation. With successful applications, data augmentation is now an established technique in NLP, and we hope this study will inspire more theoretical investigations on the subject. As the field continues to evolve, we expect more effective data augmentation techniques to be developed, allowing wider adoption in practical NLP projects. In particular, augmentations sensitive to labeled data can be used to create more robust models that much better handle data quality issues. Additionally, models trained with such augmentations may be more resistant to distribution shifts in new, unseen data. Finally, we observe that data augmentation models inherently incorporate both data quality awareness and distribution shift awareness, suggesting they have great potential to handle a wide range of practical NLP tasks.

Recent action proposal models have achieved high precision but are limited by slow computation due to extensive use of spatial pyramid pooling. To balance speed and accuracy, we introduce the Dual Context Aggregation Network (DCAN), which uses two context aggregation modules to simultaneously extract local and global context features. Unlike traditional methods that compute context features for each individual stride, DCAN uses two modules to combine local and global context features simultaneously, thus reducing computational cost and increasing efficiency. In testing mode, DCAN uses two cascade prediction modules to integrate multi-scale context features and perform classification and bounding box regression. Experimental results show that DCAN achieves higher average precision than state-of-the-art action proposal models, while being 26.9 times faster than MSRA R-FCN and 5.5 times faster than FCA at 2000 proposals, making it suitable for real-time applications. Moreover, DCAN demonstrates superior performance in instance annotation, outperforming human annotators in terms of accuracy. The code of DCAN is openly available at https://github.com/cg1177/DCAN.

By analyzing a renewal process with a tail exponent, we demonstrate the existence of a quenched large deviation principle for random point processes that arise from a non-stationary renewal process. This result applies to models of DNA sequences and holds locally in time. Furthermore, when the renewal process has a power-law tail with an exponent greater than one, we prove the existence of a quenched large deviation principle for the distribution of letter frequencies. If the tail exponent is greater than two, we show that the stationary measure of the renewal process exhibits a bimodal structure. Additionally, for a specific model of DNA sequences with dinucleotide dependencies, we obtain a bimodal structure for the measure of local point processes and demonstrate that the stationary measure of letter frequencies has a bimodal structure. This measures the strength of selective pressure on single nucleotides and dinucleotides. The bimodal structure of the measure of local point processes was previously proven by Pemantle and Peres (2000) for an independent sequence. Our results provide a quantitative analysis of their findings. The methods used in this study also allow us to derive rates for the large deviations and a characterization of the minimizing measures of the large deviation principle. The latter reveals the existence of an optimal renewal scheme that approximates the quenched large deviation principle. This leads to an algorithm that can generate renewal processes with the desired large deviation property and, in particular, sequences with desired letter or block frequencies. We demonstrate the efficacy of this algorithm by generating a bicritical renewal process. The methods used in this study also enable us to extend the results to a broader class of renewal processes. We conclude by discussing potential applications of our findings, including the development of benchmarks for testing statistical models of DNA sequences. We propose a new metric that can be used for this purpose and demonstrate its utility in evaluating the performance of such models. We present empirical results that compare the performance of several models, including one that exhibits a bimodal structure, and show that these models can capture essential features of actual DNA sequences without significant bias. We believe that our study will prove useful in advancing the statistical analysis of DNA sequences and inspiring new research in this field. We offer our algorithm for generating renewal processes with desired large deviation properties and several DNA sequence models that exhibit critical behavior at multiple scales. We are particularly interested in a model that exhibits a bimodal structure for the measure of letter frequencies and is comparable to actual DNA sequences. We provide our algorithm and several DNA sequence models that exhibit critical behavior at multiple scales.

Lipschitz games have been a significant area of study in dynamic games, particularly in the last two decades. A branch of related research involves quasi-concave games, which were first explored in the context of dynamic games by Blackwell in 1967. This paper delivers two main contributions. Firstly, it presents a generalization of Lipschitz games, dubbed "separable Lipschitz games," where each player's payoff function exhibits individualized Lipschitz characteristics. The study of these games builds upon existing frameworks of dynamic games. Secondly, the paper introduces an algorithm tailored for finding an equilibrium in separable Lipschitz games, which leverages the characteristics of these games, specifically the structure of their subgradients, to enhance computational efficiency. This algorithm outperforms alternative approaches, such as the method of multipliers, by eliminating the need for explicit computation of subgradients through an auxiliary function. The proposed algorithm demonstrates superior performance in a set of benchmark problems. The paper's findings are further validated through an examination of the perceived value of information in a decision-making process. The algorithm developed as part of this research can be found in the supplementary materials provided with the paper. This includes the code written in MATLAB that implements the algorithm and associated tests mentioned in the paper. The code is available upon request. The paper's results have been verified through simulation runs conducted on computing clusters at the University of Texas at Austin and the University of Michigan. Our investigation reveals that utilizing J-K-fold cross validation enhances the reliability of performance predictions when compared to traditional K-fold methods, particularly when working with a limited number of data points. To further examine this benefit, we conducted a related survey of existing literature. Additionally, we demonstrate how J-K-fold validates the stability of performance outcomes across different models, as well as how it facilitates the comparison of performance metrics with minimal reliance on random results. This, in turn, enables a more accurate evaluation of the significance of performance differences in scenarios with limited data sets. We also introduce a novel plot to visualize the robustness of performance outcomes under different J-K-fold settings. This allows researchers to effectively assess the stability of performance estimates when working with small data sets. We have made publicly available all code and data used in our study, along with a comprehensive software implementation that is compatible with R. This implementation is openly accessible on GitHub, along with a detailed documentation on our methodological approach, which is outlined in the associated manuscript. This study is in line with the ISLR3 book chapters by James et al., "An Introduction to Statistical Learning" and the related RMOOC course materials. This work is part of our ongoing research project, along with other related investigations, such as the effectiveness of J-K-fold in hyperparameter tuning.

Deep neural networks are commonly applied in various applications, including computer vision, but their complexity hinders their deployment on devices with limited resources. Distilling knowledge from a complex teacher network to a simpler student network has been shown to improve the performance of lightweight models. While collaborative Teacher-Student structures have enhanced the performance of student networks, these systems typically share information through output signals, neglecting the valuable information contained in intermediate features. This research introduces a new cooperative learning algorithm that enables a teacher and student network to exchange features at various levels, successfully leveraging the valuable information in intermediate features. The proposed method uses a global average pooling layer to gather intermediate features from the teacher network and use them as additional training data for the student network. Experimental results demonstrate that this cooperative learning algorithm can boost the performance of lightweight student networks by at least 4% across various vision tasks, including MNIST, SVHN, and CIFAR-100, in comparison to standard knowledge distillation. Furthermore, this approach has a notable advantage of reducing the student network complexity by 15% while maintaining high accuracy in image classification tasks. Code is available at: https://github.com/zwang84/Cooperative-Knowledge-Distillation. The proposed cooperative learning algorithm has the potential to enhance the performance of lightweight models and make them more suitable for deployment on resource-constrained devices. The algorithm's ability to extract intermediate features from the teacher network, in addition to the output signals, facilitates a more efficient compression of the teacher network. The successful application of this algorithm is demonstrated through experiments conducted on popular vision datasets, showcasing its effectiveness in boosting the performance of lightweight student networks. The code for the cooperative learning algorithm has been made publicly available, enabling further research and development in this area. The proposed cooperative learning algorithm provides a comprehensive framework for compressing deep neural networks and can be adapted to various compression techniques, such as pruning, weighting, and quantization. The algorithm's successful application to a super-resolution task highlights its potential to enhance the performance of highly compressed networks. The public release of the code facilitates the comparison of order information among different cooperative learning algorithms, thus contributing to a deeper understanding of the proposed algorithm. The code has significant value in the deep neural network community, addressing the challenge of deploying complex deep neural networks on devices with limited resources. The publicly available code enables researchers to explore knowledge distillation as a compression technique and facilitates comparison among different compression orders. The code's potential to model order information and the proposed framework for compressing deep neural networks will spark further research and discussion in the community.

Bucket Elimination (BE) is an efficient algorithm for solving a variety of problems, like finding the most likely explanation and optimal configuration, by combining these tasks through a common objective function - often referred to as the "energy" or "cost" function. This paper offers a broader perspective on BE by demonstrating its applications across multiple domains. We specifically discuss its use cases within areas like probabilistic modeling, constraint satisfaction, and multi-criteria decision analysis. Furthermore, we illustrate the connections between BE and other related techniques, such as Survey Propagation, Distributed Constraint Reasoning, and Multi-Agent Reasoning. We also examine the issues of scaling and over-scaling in BE and explore alternative approaches that offer more balanced performance. Through practical examples and experimental results, we showcase the implications of these challenges for BE's effectiveness. This research provides BE with a unifying framework and offers potential future directions for its development and execution strategies. All BE source code and data used in this study are now freely available at https://github.com/SameerSingh/BucketElimination. This work has been publicly accessible under https://arxiv.org/abs/1709.06935 since September 2017.

We have determined the universal critical behaviors of both isotropic jamming under frictionless conditions and shear jamming with respect to friction. Isotropic jamming exhibits a continuous phase transition at $\phi_j=0.647 \pm 0.001$, with a $d=3$ dimensional elasticity critical exponent of $\delta=1.00 \pm 0.05$. Shear jamming, on the other hand, displays a first-order phase transition at $\phi_s^*=\phi_s^{\textrm{lat}} \approx 0.794$, with no distinct elasticity exponent. The distinct features of these jamming transitions may be understood in terms of the stability of certain equilibrium states, and are supported by calculations of the shear modulus and potential energy of jammed packings as functions of the friction coefficient. These findings provide a thorough theoretical foundation for understanding the universal characteristics of jamming in three-dimensional space.

We examine the potential of a TeV-scale muon collider to facilitate production of various particles through processes like pair creation of heavy long-lived particles, leptoquark-mediated processes, and cascade decays of supersymmetric particles, as well as direct production of top and bottom quarks and stable charged particles. In doing so, we investigate the relevance of these processes to currently available data and assess the necessary detector components for their observation. Our design considerations for these production processes inform the broader goals of the Muon Collider Program. Furthermore, we outline key research opportunities and propose experiments to investigate the resulting particle spectra. Additionally, we discuss the influence of process-specific background factors on the required luminosity and detection strategies. We also present preliminary estimates for necessary detector characteristics, including solid angle coverage, energy resolution, and identification capabilities for various particles and decay channels. These estimates will serve as a basis for further development of the Muon Collider detector concept. 

This work was initiated at the 2021 Workshop on Physics and Detectors at Future Muon Colliders, and we present an update on ongoing research. We highlight potential paths for research and encourage contributions from the broader scientific community. 

In addition to the main focus on production processes, we also explore direct detection of dark matter and consider multiple scenarios for dark photon production. We have identified several research opportunities that could be investigated with a muon collider, even in the absence of a fully functional collider. These opportunities include studying dark matter direct detection in pair production of heavy long-lived particles, examining the spectrum of dark photons in various cascade decays, and investigating the direct production of dark matter in the form of stable charged particles. We have also identified potential paths for enhancing the sensitivity of these research opportunities through the use of optimized reconstruction techniques, finite-lifetime analyses, and manipulation of the dark photon mass scale. We plan to delve deeper into these research opportunities in future studies.

This model allows for the modification of the projector's point-spread function within the reconstructed image, rather than being locked to the specific geometry of the acquisition device. The rCASPR method is particularly effective in reducing the negative effects of aliasing, particularly in high-frequency regions, and is capable of operating with non-rotated projections. The algorithm's robustness is showcased through applications involving MRI imaging processes. However, calculating exact p-values is computationally intensive for large samples, while Monte Carlo estimates can be inaccurate with large test sizes. We've developed a fast, exact algorithm to determine p-values, using a partitioning strategy that exploits the structure of paired data. Our algorithm generates p-value estimates up to 10,000 times faster than the Monte Carlo method for similar precision. We've also created a user-friendly R package called PPPR that makes it easy to perform paired-permutation tests and run the exact algorithm. The package is available on CRAN and can be accessed via the PPPR R package. By implementing an efficient exact method and user-friendly code, we've made it possible to accurately compare paired data at a reasonable computational cost. Additionally, we've applied this method to an analysis of treatment effectiveness in cancer patients. This study examines the recent collapse of shipping cartels known as shipping alliances through analysis of alliance behavior from 2009 to 2020. We combine a unique dataset of alliance members with theoretical models of cooperative behavior. We find that the breakdown of alliances led to increased freight rates and shipping quantities among carriers. Notably, the decline in cooperation accelerated in the last half of the period studied. We also find that carriers' incentives to collaborate have fluctuated in response to changes in alliance size and shipping patterns. Specifically, smaller alliances face greater challenges in achieving mutually beneficial outcomes, while carriers may prioritize cooperation in larger alliances where there are more opportunities for freeriding. We observe a shift towards smaller alliances in recent years, which may contribute to the accelerated decline in cooperation. We suggest that carriers' strategies to mitigate freeriding could explain the accelerated decline in cooperation seen in the second half of the study period. We further explore the implications of our findings for antitrust policy in the shipping industry. We suggest that Alliance behavior may vary sufficiently to justify case-by-case antitrust analysis. We also consider the potential benefits to consumers of facilitating cooperation among carriers in specific situations. We argue that any analysis of Alliance behavior should account for the complex, dynamic nature of Alliance relationships. We draw parallels between the shipping industry and traditional views on cartel behavior, where large, stable relationships between buyers and sellers can differ substantially from the fleeting connections characteristic of freerriding situations. We propose that the structure of the shipping industry, complete with frequent port calls and temporary relationships between carriers and ship captains, may contribute to the challenges Alliance members face in maintaining cooperation. We speculate that advances in information technology, along with changing global trade patterns, may have contributed to the decline in cooperation among Alliance members. We anticipate that the complex, dynamic nature of Alliance behavior in the shipping industry will continue to evolve in response to these changes. Graph neural networks (GNNs) have consistently demonstrated superiority over traditional deep learning techniques in processing complex data structured as graphs. Researchers often attribute GNN success to graph structure itself, yet there's a lack of investigation into the relative importance of graph structure versus node features within GNNs. We challenge this inquiry by presenting a novel training method aimed at maximizing the impact of graph structure over node features, achieving results that surpass baseline performances in multiple benchmark datasets according to our experimental findings. Our technique involves a unique loss function that penalizes model predictions on modified graphs with altered node features, allowing us to control the influence of graph structure versus node features. We further develop a systematic approach to determining optimal model parameters through a batching strategy for efficient evaluation. Our technique demonstrates a notable advantage in our experiments, achieving performance improvements for both link prediction and node classification tasks on Mutag, AIDS, and PPI datasets. The open-source code is available for replication and future research on our technique. Overall, our approach provides a significant contribution to understanding the performance of GNNs and offers a powerful technique for maximizing graph structure's effect over node features.

In this research, we examine an alternative approach that adapts the input itself, rather than just the variable selection, and develop new procedures for estimating parameters and evaluating the effectiveness of this approach. Notably, our results demonstrate that this adaptive input method yields more robust traditional estimators compared to non-adaptive approaches, particularly in scenarios with limited data. Additionally, we find that the benefits of adapting the input outweigh the drawbacks in high-dimensional scenarios, without causing the issues of an overfitting parameter. This contrast highlights the unique thermodynamic properties of vortex cores, which can lead to an increase in local heat capacity and a shift in the melting line of the vortex lattice in superconductors. Numerical results for the entropy and heat capacity within a vortex core have been derived for a London superconductor and a BSCCO crystal, demonstrating that the thermodynamic properties of vortex cores can distinguish between intravalley and intervalley excitations. These distinct features of vortex cores may provide a thermodynamic basis for experimentally distinguishing between these two types of excitations. Furthermore, our study indicates that the formation of the vortex lattice phase can be identified by analyzing the melting line's curvature, which is influenced by the strength of correlation between the order parameter and the vector potential. Additionally, we find that the heat capacity within a vortex core can exhibit an anomalous peak at the melting line, which may be a hallmark of a first-order transition in the vortex lattice. Lastly, our findings also imply that the motion of magnetic flux lines could give rise to a thermal Hall effect in superconductors with non-trivial Berry phases.

We introduce a new coordinate gauge in the vicinity of a non-relativistic static point mass within a spherically symmetric spacetime. This 'pre-non-relativistic' parametrization aids in expanding metric components and their derivatives in a relativistic gravitational context. We demonstrate that, as a first approach, the metric can be approximated by incorporating boundary conditions that ensure the absence of divergent terms at the point of singularity. Consequently, we believe this method may provide a suitable framework for examining non-classical features of point-like objects, such as metric fluctuations due to quantum effects, in general relativity. To support this, we show that a perturbative analytical expansion of metric components can be achieved using the 'pre-non-relativistic' coordinates, resulting in an acceptable agreement when compared to numerical solutions of relativistic static point masses. The metric components obtained from this method also exhibit the expected behavior of non-relativistic gravitational potentials, thus allowing for the identification of the non-relativistic metric parameters, such as the mass and the non-relativistic potential energy, which can be expressed as an integral of the spacetime mass density. Notably, we observe that, in contrast to conventional non-relativistic theories, the spacetime mass density in general relativity has an additional non-linear component related to the gravitational potential energy itself. Consequently, the usual superposition principle no longer applies no the masses generating such a spacetime, and an analytical expansion of metric components with respect to the number of point masses becomes necessary for its accuracy. As a by-product, we also derive the spacetime mass density in the presence of a non-interacting fermionic gas at finite temperature, providing a new means of investigating the spacetime mass density in general relativity. Ultimately, we propose that the 'pre-non-relativistic' parametrization may offer a suitable coordinate gauge for examining the spacetime mass density in non-linear general relativity. The proposed approach could have a broader implications for investigating the spacetime mass density in non-linear general relativity, particularly in the presence of non-linear interactions, such as those involving fermionic fields, and may provide a new means of understanding the spacetime mass density in relation to the gravitational field itself. The 'pre-non-relativistic' parametrization appears to be an effective tool for analyzing the spacetime mass density in non-linear general relativity, and the study of metric fluctuations due to quantum effects, such as those associated with the behavior of the gravitational field in the context of the Casimir effect

This study explores the properties of minimum density power divergence (MDPD) estimators in conjunction with ML (maximum likelihood) estimators for various processes, including independent increment and Markov processes. We examine the theoretical differences and similarities between these two sets of estimators based on the DP (density power divergence) family and establish the relationship between their parameters. We also investigate the practical implications of these findings through simulations and a real-world example. Specifically, we compare the performance of MDPD and ML estimators in modeling independent increment processes, assess the performance of MDPD estimators with varying parameters in conjunction with ML estimators for Markov processes, examine the performance of MDPD estimators with parameters optimized for minimum loss function in conjunction with ML estimators for these processes, and apply these results to MDPD estimators with optimized parameters. We demonstrate that MDPD estimators can be a viable alternative to ML estimators, offering comparable or even better performance in modeling these processes. The central engines of active galaxies, including quasars and blazars, exhibit extreme energy released compared to that in typical active galactic nuclei. This energy is insufficiently explained by current models and might be partially resolved by the presence of shocks caused by massive gas accretion, which would also account for the broad emission lines observed in these objects. To better comprehend the physical conditions within these regions, we utilize a grid of 3D chemical simulations tailored to active galaxies. These simulations encompass various elemental species and involve multiple scenarios for shock-ionization patterns. To identify distinctive signatures of shock-ionization, we compared our results to those obtained from the standard photoionization model of the (ionizing spectrum of) very massive stars. The comparisons revealed several notable features emerging from shock-ionization: (1) a prominent increase in the mass of high-temperature gas, (2) broader and more irregular emission line profiles, (3) the appearance of faint [O III] $\lambda$5007 emission behind the broad [O II] $\lambda$3727, (4) a shift in the maximum of the [O III] $\lambda$5007 line towards shorter wavelengths, (5) larger clumps with larger internal temperature gradients and molecular gas content, and (6) faster gas clump velocities. These characteristics offer potential observational indicators of shock-ionization and could also influence the detection of heavy elements, such as iron, by altering the abundance ratios of a particular gas clump. Furthermore, they may provide insights into the gas accretion rate and the presence of molecular gas. If prevalent in active galaxies, shock-ionization could also help resolve certain discrepancies between observed and predicted spectral characteristics, specifically the intensity of [O III] $\lambda$5007. The distinctive features of shock-ionization also depend on the relationship between the shock speed and the ionizing radiation distance, which can serve as yet another diagnostic tool for active galaxies. The variations in ionization conditions within these objects could result in the emergence of two distinct populations of active galaxies, separating low- and high-ionization areas, and possibly even shedding light on the nature of ultra-luminous active galaxies that resemble quasars. The influence of shock-ionization on heavy elements also raises the possibility of observing iron lines at much closer distances to the central engine than currently achievable. By conditioning intermediate representations on scene maps, SceneGen successfully navigates the complex interactions between all scene elements. Through evaluations using the NGSIM dataset and a comparison with recent object-generation models, our approach has demonstrated superior performance in modeling individual objects and overall scene accuracy. The Finite Element Method (FEM) offers a versatile numerical approach for solving various partial differential equations (PDEs). Specifically, we introduce an inner product modification that leads to more accurate iterations. We demonstrate multiple ways to derive this modification, including drawing from inner product space theory. Furthermore, we provide explicit formulas for computing both the standard and modified FGMRES residuals. We also investigate several example use cases, involving nonlinear problems and the time-dependent heat equation, to showcase the benefits of the modified iteration. Our results indicate that the proposed approach yields greater convergence and precision compared to the standard FGMRES. We implement the algorithm using the FEniCS framework and offer our modified FGMRES iteration as a publicly accessible tool via the PyGMTS library. We also explore various parameters of the algorithm, including the use of a preconditioner, and present guidelines for selecting optimal parameters for different problems. We address two prominent conjectures in topological dynamics: the Fixed Point Conjecture and the Orbit Separation Conjecture. these massive clouds may give rise to superbubbles with complex structures, affecting

dust emission maps. The findings indicate that the structure of superbubbles is

dust temperature within superbubbles when comparing observed values to theoretical models. Moreover, a significant discrepancy is noted between the predicted and observed
distribution of gas across the disk. In addition, a correlation between the size of
superbubbles and the maximum velocity spread in radio recombination line spectra is
identified, implying that the expansion of superbubbles may be influenced by the
presence of large-scale magnetic fields. The detection of varying dust temperatures
within superbubbles suggests that there may be additional energy inputs affecting the
heating of dust across different regions within these massive molecular clouds. The
duration of these interactions could potentially provide insights into the history of
the interactions within these clouds. The complex structure of superbubbles, coupled
with the significant dust mass within these clouds, may have implications for the
formation and evolution of massive star clusters and the surrounding interstellar
medium. The effects of pair-instability and core-collapse supernovae on the structure
of superbubbles also raise the possibility that the formation of massive molecular
clouds may be influenced directly by the feedback from these extreme events. The
study of the dynamics within these massive molecular clouds can offer a more
direct view of the interactions occurring within them, and thus, the suitable targets
for such studies should be observed simultaneously in both radio recombination
lines and submillimeter dust emission to gain a comprehensive understanding of
their structure and evolution. The suitable candidates for such observations can
be selected from the existing datasets, and new targets can be identified through
a statistical analysis of the spatial distribution of the newly formed massive star
clusters across the galactic plane. The suitable targets for these observations
are likely to include regions like the W3 and W4 molecular clouds, as well as the

While significant progress has been made in self-supervised flow estimation, significant obstacles remain in this field. Notably, current approaches struggle to handle occlusions, a common issue that can severely impede the performance of other computer vision tasks. To mitigate this limitation, we propose a novel framework for unoccluded self-supervised flow estimation that utilizes an auxiliary decoder. This additional component produces a synthetic image to complement the actual input image, and is trained to reconstruct an artificial version of the missing regions. As a result, our method achieves enhanced performance by minimizing the influence of occlusions, thereby producing more accurate and unoccluded synthetic images that can be utilized for self-supervised learning. Moreover, our proposed framework offers greater flexibility, as it allows for the generation of unoccluded synthetic images directly from the input image, bypassing the need for forward and backward passes through the encoder. Combining these strategies, we introduce a new self-supervised flow estimation method that incorporates an auxiliary decoder, and validate our approach by conducting extensive experiments on the MT167K, ADE20K, and COCO flow datasets, showcasing superior performance compared to existing state-of-the-art methods. These are the cubic graphs that can be divided into two components with identical structures, with each vertex appearing in exactly one of these components. We explore the property of even-2-factorability in cubic graphs, establishing a connection to circulant matrices. A crucial finding emerges from this connection - a cubic graph is even-2-factorable if and only if its adjacency matrix can be expressed as the square of a real circulant matrix. We employ this relationship to provide a novel proof for the existence of even 2-factors in cubic graphs, building upon a previous circumvention of Gallyardt's theorem. Furthermore, we introduce an algorithm to determine the structure of an even 2-factor in a cubic graph, enabled by the real circulant matrix representation. This leads to further insights into the structure of an even 2-factor and its association with the graph's circulant matrix properties. We also establish a connection between the number of even 2-factors and the number of positive eigenvalues of the graph's adjacency matrix. Additionally, we introduce the concept of half-2-factorable graphs, exploring their properties and establishing a connection to circulant matrices with real entries only. We conclude by discussing several open questions related to even-2-factorable and half-2-factorable graphs. These questions revolve around the structure of these graphs, their circulant matrix representation, and the existence of certain graph substructures. These problems are sure to stimulate further research in this engaging field of study.

This paper introduces a novel technique called Timeloops, which enables the optional omission of system calls from specific regions of programs. Unlike conventional system call introspection methods, Timeloops is designed to work with programs written in interpreted languages, utilizing dynamic binary instrumentation to monitor system calls in real-time, even when the program is running normally without any special privileges. We demonstrate the effectiveness of Timeloops by applying it to popular web servers and databases written in PHP and Python, showing that a significant proportion of system calls can be safely skipped without compromising program correctness. Furthermore, Timeloops is revealed to offer significant performance gains for workloads characterized by prolonged system call pauses. In particular, it achieves speedups of up to 42% for systems calls that can be avoided and reduces the average slowdown due to system calls from 0.21 seconds to less than 0.01 seconds. We also explore various architectures that can build upon Timeloops's system call skipping functionality to deliver even greater performance benefits. As proof of concept, we develop a timeriting compiler patch for the Zephyr operating system, which, along with our results from the GNU/Linux platform, validates the feasibility of Timeloops. Lastly, we outline several avenues for further research and potential applications of Timeloops, including memory safety, operating system components, and entire operating systems. The way sports are covered by the media is undergoing a shift from traditional reporting to in-depth data analysis. This transformation's impact on sports such as football is being explored in the present study. We delved into the specifics of the 2020 UEFA European Football Championship, utilizing the available data from the tournament's website, to investigate the underlying factors that influence the awarding of free kicks from defensive actions within the game. Our research involved using reward assignment via expected outcome (RAEO) to determine the assigned rewards for actions like committing a foul or causing the ball to go out by comparing them to attempting a shot on goal in various game scenarios. We also conducted an action clustering method to identify patterns in the actions leading to free kicks and found that the assigned rewards varied significantly based on the location and player involvement. Notably, scoring a goal was compared to gaining the opposing team as a reward. By executing a data visualization technique known as parallel sets, we presented the distribution of rewards for the actions leading to free kicks graphically. The findings suggested that players often prioritize minimizing penalties over scoring goals, especially when the game's outcome is not certain; however, when a significant advantage is at stake, they are more inclined to take risks. Additionally, the rewards for the actions leading to free kicks varied based on the location on the field, especially for shooting, while the influences of player involvement were less pronounced. The study's findings can benefit teams and managers in making strategic decisions during games, while the approach used could be applied to any situation where the outcome of an action is evaluated based on a set of base rewards. We are conducting a study on Full Waveform Inversion (FWI) using time-domain wavefields within a time-domain optimization framework. This review aims to examine potential issues with time-domain FWI, including the generation of local minima and the presence of non-physical solutions. We argue that non-physical solutions can be managed by applying a T-t symmetry constraint to the wave equation. Additionally, we propose a method for reducing local minima by introducing a time-averaged stress tensor in the objective function. This approach, however, is associated with an increased computational demand. We also derive an explicit formula for the time-averaged stress tensor that can be used to simplify the inversion process. We demonstrate the feasibility of our method through numerical simulations conducted on synthetic models. The results show that averaging the stress tensor over time yields the best possible solution in cases of mild nonlinearity, whereas further simulations reveal the emergence of local minima in more nonlinear scenarios. We further show that incorporating the time-averaged stress tensor leads to a significant improvement in the accuracy of the stress tensor estimation. Nevertheless, we observe the appearance of non-physical solutions in some cases and propose using the symmetry constraint to mitigate this issue. Moreover, we found that FWI for the density variable typically converges to the correct solution, whereas the convergence for the other variables depends on the dispersion parameter. We also discovered that increasing the sampling rate improves the convergence but introduces discrete artifacts. We conclude by highlighting the potential for further research on time-domain FWI.

This research examines an asymmetric noisy voter model where two species compete on a lattice, with the possibility of switching between species being inaccurate. We analyze the model's dynamics on a square lattice and demonstrate that, regardless of the precision of the switching process, only two outcomes are possible: both species coexist indefinitely, or one species dominates and eventually supplants the other. The precise conditions for these outcomes, as well as the exact condition for accuracy-driven switching that leads to coexistence, are derived. Additionally, our findings are validated through numerical simulations and the effects of varying the precision of switching are illustrated. Furthermore, our analysis is expanded to include the impact of an external influence promoting the switch to the alternative species, and it is found that this leads to the demise of one species, regardless of the precision of the switching process. The applicability of our model to biological systems is discussed, and our calculations are compared with empirical data from the evolution of ant colonies. Our study provides new insights into the asymmetric noisy voter model, as well as the related process of the inhomogeneous directed percolation process, and its implications for our understanding of biological system evolution. Lastly, our research highlights the significance of considering the inaccuracies inherent to biological processes.
