Recent studies in generating counterfactual data have primarily focused on enhancing model performance. In contrast, we introduce DISCO, a novel framework that allows for the creation of counterfactual data to improve the robustness of machine learning models. By leveraging a diverse range of real world data, DISCO generates counterfactual data that is distinct from real data and effectively simulates real-world data variations, thereby enhancing model robustness. Our experimental results demonstrate that training models with counterfactual data generated by DISCO improves their robustness and generalization performance, particularly in complex scenarios such as out-of-distribution predictions and distributed training. Furthermore, our studies reveal that these robust models are capable of reducing the gap between observed disparities and real-world disparities, thereby exhibiting lower bias. Our findings also suggest that DISCO-generated counterfactual data can be highly effective in promoting model robustness, with no additional cost. In particular, our experiments across multiple datasets reveal that training models with counterfactual data generated by DISCO yields a robustness gain of over 20% in certain scenarios. Our research also highlights the underlying challenges faced by current counterfactual generation methods, which often produce stilted examples that differ significantly from real data. In contrast, DISCO-generated counterfactual data exhibits a much closer similarity to real data, thereby further contributing to the improvement in model robustness. Our framework DISCO offers a novel perspective on counterfactual data generation, shifting the focus from enhancing model performance to promoting model robustness. In doing so, our research highlights the distinction between counterfactual data that is effective in boosting robustness and that which is merely model-performing. In the process, our studies have been enriched with real-world data from diverse sources, including web images and text. Ultimately, our work paves the way for a critical reevaluation of the goals and methodologies of counterfactual data generation, with implications for the development of more robust machine learning models. The equitable coloring number EC(G) is the minimum number of colors required for an equitable coloring. The total equitable coloring number TEC(G) is the minimum number of colors required for a total equitable coloring, where each color has the same frequency in each neighborhood and each vertex also has a distinct color from its neighbors. The total sum distinguishing coloring number TSDC(G) is a proper coloring where the sum of colors on each vertex is distinct in each neighborhood and each vertex also has a distinct sum from its neighbors. The neighborhood sum distinguishing total coloring number NSDTC(G) is a proper coloring where the sum of colors on each vertex is distinct in each neighborhood. Some general results about these colorings are derived and some specific cases are determined. Circulant graphs that are complete graphs or bipartite graphs are exceptions because they require no coloring and all vertices share the same sum or frequency in each neighborhood respectively. We've observed a temperature-dependent phenomenon in the MBE growth of InAs on a graphene substrate, where varying the temperature leads to distinct microstructures.  At higher growth temperatures, a pattern consisting of numerous small epitaxial domains exists, while lower temperatures result in larger, less complex areas.  By combining MM-GWR and SEM-GWR, along with electrical characterization, we've determined that higher growth temperatures cause the formation of multiple low-barrier domains due to the reduced size of the Coherent Domain, which is likely influenced by the increased thermal vibration of atoms, resulting in a weaker alignment between the InAs and graphene at growth sites.  This thermal energy allows for the relaxation of strained InAs islands within the domains, ultimately leading to the observed smaller sizes.  As a result, the electrical properties, specifically the RT Hall conductivity, exhibit optimal values at intermediate temperatures.  This research reveals the thermal effects on the InAs/graphene interaction and suggests the possibility of precise control over the epitaxial structure through temperature adjustment, thereby opening up new avenues for the design of graphene-based heterostructures.  We propose that this temperature-dependent phenomenon may provide a useful paradigm for exploring new physics in graphene-based systems through controlled variations in epitaxial structures.  We also suggest potential applications for this phenomenon, including the systematic investigation of quantum states in devices with large epitaxial areas and the development of highly sensitive Hall devices utilizing large, low-barrier domains.  We propose that the precise control offered by this temperature-dependent approach could significantly contribute to the development of graphene-based technology.  We anticipate that this new perspective on the interaction between strain and vibration in epitaxial systems will stimulate further research and experimentation.  We look forward to exploring the outcomes of these investigations and the potential they hold for the future of graphene-based technology. Main idea:  In the process of creating multi-label data, a single relevant label can significantly accelerate annotation. This acceleration is made possible by identifying a key characteristic of each category. Based on this characteristic, a sampling strategy is proposed that efficiently finds a primary label for each new data sample. The proposed approach, single-to-multi-label (S2M) sampling, is an effective way to generate multi-label data with reduced annotation costs.

Method overview:  The proposed S2M sampling strategy is a method for finding a single characteristic-based label for each data sample. This strategy is part of a more comprehensive multi-label data generation framework, which uses the found primary label as a starting point for further iteration to obtain a set of relevant labels.

Key component:  The proposed attribute-based multi-label search (ATM-S) classifier is an efficient solution for multi-label classification. This classifier is characterized by its ability to find a single label that best matches the characteristic of each data sample, with the option to iterate multiple times to obtain a set of relevant labels.

Results:  The proposed S2M sampling strategy was evaluated in terms of its annotation efficiency and compared to other sampling methods. The findings indicate that the proposed approach not only reduces annotation costs but also results in a more accurate multi-label classifier.

To address criticisms of the simple one-zone model used for gamma-ray studies, a more advanced model has been developed that accounts for electron heating and cooling. In a numerical investigation, the model was refined to better capture high-energy observations. The modified model includes an electron heating term in the energy equation and assumes energy equilibrium between electrons and magnetic fields. A closing equation is achieved by introducing a minimum energy threshold for magnetic fluctuations. The model was applied to the JCMT daily maps of G339.85+0.55 to investigate its effectiveness. By correlating gamma-ray energies with magnetic fluctuations, the model was able to reproduce the gamma-ray spectra observed by MAGIC at energies greater than approximately 1 GeV. However, at lower energies, the model underestimates the observed gamma-ray flux. The model's variability was also compared to the gamma-ray data, showing a daily variability similar to that observed by MAGIC, but at a higher amplitude. The model's performance is sensitive to the electron heating rate, which must be greater than unity to replicate the gamma-ray spectra. The model also fails to account for gamma-ray energies below approximately 1 GeV and may not adequately capture magnetic energies at this energy range. Further research is needed to clarify these shortcomings. The model may be refined to better tackle these issues and provide a more comprehensive explanation of the gamma-ray data. This paper introduces a new model for the distribution of cross-sectional stock returns, which is a two-parameter model based on the Euler method of integrating asset pricing equations. The model is unique in that it is an integral-based closure model, closing the loop on the pricing equation by incorporating the moments of the returns distribution. The paper demonstrates that the four initial moments of the cross-sectional returns distribution are equivalent to the corresponding moments of the asset returns distribution, providing a direct link between the returns distribution and asset pricing equations. The model includes a derivation of the closed-form expression for the fourth moment of cross-sectional returns and an analysis of the pricing implications for assets with skewness and kurtosis. The paper further includes an empirical study of the returns distribution of the S&P 500 index, supporting the application of the model. Recently, advanced cardiac abnormality detection based on deep learning has gained significant interest. Yet, deep learning models are prone to being influenced by their training data and may not effectively identify conditions in environments they've never encountered. To overcome this limitation, the introduction of a new model that can learn from limited clean training images and adapt to handle noisy input data is presented. The proposed noise-adaptive deep neural network (NADNN) models a conditional probability of output noise given input images and integrates this model into its architecture. By training the NADNN in an unsupervised manner with clean training data, the model can learn to capture the data distribution. The training of the noise model is then modified to the task at hand - identifying conditions in noisy environments. The proposed NADNN is evaluated on two publicly available datasets and demonstrates superior performance when compared to current state-of-the-art approaches. The experimental results show the benefits of the proposed approach in detecting cardiac mrmo and audio signals from various types of noise. The increasing use of wearable devices for activity monitoring produces rich data, yet many existing methods fail to achieve satisfactory performance when applied to real-world data. This performance shortfall is attributed to overfitting caused by training on abundant data with limited labels. To address this issue, we propose FedHealth, a novel multi-client federated learning framework for wearable activity recognition. By incorporating an activity-induced bias term in the model, FedHealth successfully reduces overfitting and delivers better than expected results, outperforming conventional approaches when evaluated on the Wearable Physiology Dataset. The framework's effectiveness is further confirmed by the superior performance of FedHealth in a comprehensive comparison with leading federated learning techniques. The source code for FedHealth is available online. To facilitate further research, we also introduce a new dataset known as HospitalActivity Dataset, which was collected through wearable devices and contains data related to various hospital activities. A existence and uniqueness result for the reflected solution is derived, along with an analysis of the optimal payoff in the case of a constant interest rate. Furthermore, an option pricing model is developed to value a European put option, with results comparing the impact of different underlying diffusions. Numerical valuation of European put options is presented for various parameters. The study also explores the effect of increasing volatility on option values, both with and without the influence of the diffusion. The findings demonstrate that the value of options can be significantly affected by the presence of the underlying diffusion, with possible strategies for risk management. The study is set within the context of a financial market model comprising one stock and two bonds, with the option price dependent on the initial stock price and time. The research highlights the importance of considering the underlying diffusion process when valuing options, with implications for how risk is managed and priced in financial markets. The study also highlights the need for further research into option pricing models, given the complex effects observed between option values, volatility, and the underlying diffusion process. Understanding how gene expression changes over time is crucial for identifying essential variables that influence this process. By drawing parallels to traditional static variable learning problems, researchers have explored a method called submodular maximization to establish bounds on the efficiency of finding key variables in time-dependent gene expression data. However, this approach requires significant computational resources due to the large dimensionality of the data. To address this issue, we introduce an approximate optimization technique based on relevance learning that significantly reduces computational costs by only considering previously identified variables. The proposed algorithm, called ASMTF, selectively adds the most influential variables in each time point, prioritizing those that have the greatest impact on previously selected variables. We demonstrate the effectiveness of ASMTF through both synthetic and real-world experiments, showcasing its ability to strike a balance between efficiency and accuracy. Interestingly, we found that ASMTF often surpasses the performance of the more computationally expensive submodular maximization technique. Additionally, ASMTF displayed a high degree of scalability when handling large datasets. To facilitate reproducibility, the source code for ASMTF is now available online. Moreover, we incorporated an R package called RMTF that provides an easy-to-use implementation of ASMTF, along with other related algorithms. We also included a set of predefined parameters and metrics to streamline the evaluation process. We also introduced a new metric called the geometric mean of ratios (GMR), which provides a more comprehensive understanding of the temporal expression profiles. An intriguing set of galaxies known as Distant White Dwarfs offers a singular 
opportunity for studying the surroundings of extremely bright galaxies. By analyzing 
the [OIII] emissions at [OIII]~51bm, we examined a sample of 11 Distant White 
Dwarfs, discovering a notable variation in the CI line ratios among three of 
these galaxies. These variations can be attributed to the presence of low-density 
molecular wind or circumgalactic gas reservoirs with characteristics similar to 
those found in extreme starburst galaxies, such as M82. Furthermore, we observed 
a correlation between the 36bm/51bm CI line ratio and the starburst distance from 
the central black hole, suggesting that the molecular gas within these galaxies 
remains relatively stable despite the presence of a supermassive black hole. We 
also discovered evidence supporting the external fueling theory of active nuclear 
regions, where the atomic gas near the nuclear region is likely fueled by the 
presence of an extensive molecular gas reservoir. This finding is consistent with 
observations in the Arp 220 galaxy. Additionally, we found that the atomic gas 
within these galaxies exhibits variations in both velocity and density, featuring 
turbulent motion and complex structure. A comparison with local galaxies reveals 
a difference in both CI line ratios and atomic gas properties, suggesting that 
Distant White Dwarfs are distinct from local galaxies and requiring further 
theoretical modeling to better understand these extremely bright galaxies. These 
results were achieved through combining data from the Hubble Space Telescope, 
Spitzer, and ALMA, as well as the use of custom-made atomic gas analysis 
software. This study offers a unique perspective on the atomic and molecular gas 
within extremely bright galaxies, offering a window into the complex physics and 
gas dynamics at play. This research was conducted by a team of scientists led by

The phenomenon of lepton-flavor universality (LFU) has been examined in various decay processes such as $K$ and $B$ meson decays. Given the observed disparities in flavor, one possible explanation is the involvement of a fourth generation of particles with lepton-flavor interacting weakly. In this analysis, we prioritize the explanation of flavor anomalies seen in $K$, $B$, and $\bar{B}$ meson decays and investigate the properties of the corresponding vector bosons. We consider several scenarios for the anomalies, which may involve the presence of a dark sector, lepton-flavour non-universality, or rare decays mediated by gluons or scalar fields. By examining the anomalies in a broader context, we find that the majority can be accounted for by assuming the existence of new $B$ and $K$ meson scalar particles, which however, would significantly impact the $B$ meson sector. On the other hand, vector bosons with masses in the TeV range and energies around 5-10 GeV can explain the $K$ meson anomalies while also fitting with data from other decay processes. These vector bosons can also interact with leptons of other flavors but with much lower probabilities, thus explaining the observed disparities in flavor. Additionally, we propose several experiments to identify these vector bosons, including the construction of an asymmetric $B$ factory and deep underground detectors to observe the missing energy signature in the decay processes. The proposed experiments have the potential to either confirm or refute the existence of these vector bosons and thereby shed light on the explanation for the flavor anomalies in the $K$ and $B$ meson systems. This could ultimately contribute to a deeper comprehension of the principles of lepton-flavour universality. This study is the initial step in a comprehensive analysis and there are various directions that warrant further exploration. It is our hope that this analysis will spark a thorough investigation into the anomalies in the $K$ and $B$ meson decays within the context of the LFU phenomenon. This research is also accompanied by a report outlining the key findings that have been presented at the 2021 Lepton-Photon Conference. This document includes an overview of the anomalies in the $K$ and $B$ meson systems and the proposed experiments to identify the vector bosons that can explain these anomalies. This document is available in the form of a LPSC talk, which has been submitted to the arXiv server. This research is supported by the DFG

We investigate the largest intersection of two metric balls within the Cayley graph of binary strings, utilizing the Hamming distance. By formulating an integer programming problem, we aim to find the maximum number of characters that can be identical in two strings, subject to Hamming distances between specific positions being less than a certain error rate and a particular threshold. We focus on the Cayley graph under cyclic conditions, where we determine the maximum number of characters that can be the same, allowing for up to $e$ errors, for error rates $e$ from $0$ to $1$, and for distances $d$ from $0$ to $5$. For larger distances, we can determine the maximum number of characters that can be the same for certain error rates. We further investigate the maximum number of positions that can be the same for two strings, one generated randomly, for various cyclic conditions. We demonstrate that by increasing the error tolerance $e$ at a rate of $1/n$ in the Cayley graph of length $n$, the number of positions that can be the same grows in a manner consistent with a linear function of the form $Kn$. We conclude that by taking a limit of the coefficient $K$ as $n$ approaches the absolute value of either side, i.e., $K_{\infty}$, we can determine the long-term rate of growth $K_{\infty}$ of the number of positions that can be the same for two strings, one generated randomly, for specific error rates $e$ from $0.5$ to $1$. We calculate $K_{\infty}$ for error rates $e$ from $0.5$ to $1$, and conclude that for error rates greater than $1/3$, the number of positions that can be the same for two strings, one generated randomly, grows linearly with the length of the strings, albeit at a rate less than $1$. We demonstrate that this rate of growth is greater than the estimated rate of growth of the number of characters that can be predicted with an $\epsilon$-accurate prefix-free code, specifically for error probabilities $e$ from $0.5$ to $1$. This research enhances prototypical network-based music instrument classification by introducing a hierarchical loss function based on the hierarchical organization of musical instruments within categories such as families and genres. The proposed approach incorporates a hierarchical loss function with separate loss terms for each classification level, leveraging both the global and local distributions of prototypes. Our hierarchical loss function is achieved by incorporating a weighted cross-entropy loss term for each classification level, where the weights are determined by the distance between prototypes and their hierarchical neighbors. We have conducted multiple experiments using the MUSDB18 dataset in combination with an additional dataset of recording titles, obtaining superior classification accuracy compared to the baseline prototypical network model. The proposed approach has been found to be particularly effective in classifying instruments that belong to multiple categories, providing a practical solution for addressing the complexity of the music instrument classification task. The source code is available online at https://github.com/letodo/hierprotopoint.

We've derived precise and approximate forms of the detection efficiency for Pulsar Timing Array (PTA) experiments at various levels of data analysis, and validated these findings through realistic simulations. The exact efficiency formula was obtained by modeling the PTA signal and its associated noise, while the approximate forms were obtained by analyzing the characteristics of the data. We compared our approximate analytic expressions to other approaches used in PTA analyses, finding them to be equivalent or closely related to existing methods. These derived expressions can be applied to compute the detection efficiency at various analysis levels, and have been made publicly available as a user-friendly software package. By incorporating these efficient algorithms, we've achieved a significant improvement in the computational resources required for the parameter estimation technique commonly employed in PTA analyses. The improved implementation, which uses parallel processing on multiple CPU cores, has been added to the EPM package, a widely used software platform for PTA analyses. The new implementation was developed to address computational bottlenecks encountered in the non-linear signal model, particularly in the presence of highly narrow-band gravitational wave signals, and is now an open-source contribution to the EPM package. We set out to examine the velocity distribution of a distinct particle within an ASEP system, specifically one placed at position one. As time progresses from $t=0$ to $\infty$, the discrete probability $p_k(t)$ evolves in a manner that depends on the specific ASEP system under consideration. In the case of the stationary raw ASEP system, the probabilities $p_k(t)$ are directly proportional to $(k+1)\theta(k)$, where $\theta(k)$ represents the Heaviside step function. For systems driven by queue dynamics with load factor $\rho$ below unity, the probabilities $p_k(t)$ become directly proportional to $\rho^k k$, giving us a geometric distribution with a second moment of $\rho$. Conversely, should the load factor $\rho$ equal or exceed unity, the system becomes trapped at time $t=0$, resulting in a probability distribution $p_k(t) \propto (\rho^k k)^{\gamma}$, where $\gamma$ is the specific exponent that determines the system's state. We further establish that $\gamma$ can be expressed in terms of the tail of the Dirichlet distribution with specific parameters. Moreover, we establish that the disorder parameter $\tau$ for the stationary raw ASEP system is equal to three. For queue dynamics, the disorder parameter $\tau$ equals $1/\rho$. We derive the stationary raw ASEP system's second class particle velocity distribution by averaging the probability of finding a particle at position $x$ within time $\tau$. We then obtain the normalized velocity distribution $f(k)$ that is directly proportional to $(k+1)\theta(k)$. We further investigate distinct particle velocities within ASEP systems driven by queue dynamics with load factor $\rho$ below unity, obtaining a velocity distribution that is directly proportional to $\rho^k k$. Conversely, should the load factor $\rho$ equal or exceed unity, the system becomes trapped at time $t=0$, resulting in a velocity distribution that mirrors that of the system's state. We propose that such systems could provide valuable insights into the understanding of animal velocity distributions

However, modeling complexity necessitates a balance between accuracy and biological plausibility, especially when relying on fitting methods. A common approach to fit these models to data is to minimize the distance between observed and predicted values. Nevertheless, this approach often prioritizes fit over the feasibility of the model, which can lead to biased results. To address this issue, researchers have proposed an alternative method to fit these models, incorporating feasibility constraints and emphasizing the biological validity of the model. This method ensures that model predictions for key indicators, such as infection rates and demographic statistics, align with real-world data. By applying this approach to two prominent epidemiological models, our results demonstrate that even simple variants of these models can provide a good fit to data, without relying on elaborate fitting methods. Furthermore, this approach yields more biologically plausible results and predicts future cases more accurately than traditional methods. We examine the thermal behavior of linear Majorana fermions in an external linear potential by using a Gaussian distribution. This choice ensures a well-defined Fermi distribution and allows us to calculate the thermal entropy of the Majorana fermions. The effect of the linear potential on the entropy is found to be similar to that of a harmonic oscillator at temperature T, with the exception of an additional shift in the chemical potential. Specifically, the increased diffusion associated with the linear potential results in an increased entropy, which can be viewed as an enhancement of the thermal capacity. Notably, the potential to manipulate Majorana fermions through linear potentials may enable control over the thermal entropy. Furthermore, our model describes the behavior of Majorana fermions in linear potentials in the presence of harmonic potentials, such as those found in atomic chains attached to metallic surfaces. Additionally, we find that the anomalous diffusion of the conjugated field can be understood through a phase-space analysis, where the Hamiltonian dynamics govern the motion of initial coherent states. Finally, we propose that this framework could be applied to other types of zero-mode fields in topological insulators.

Acronyms pose a challenge for both humans and artificial intelligence due to their condensed and often context-dependent nature. While machine learning models can learn from examples, they frequently misunderstand acronyms that are new to them. To mitigate this issue, many systems rely on dictionaries that list acronym definitions, but these dictionaries often fall short in covering the vast spectrum of acronyms and their variations. Furthermore, the definitions provided in such dictionaries are not always up-to-date, accurate, or aligned with current language use. In addition, the processing of acronyms in natural language processing systems usually focuses solely on the acronym itself, neglecting its potential context and the fact that it is often part of a larger phrase with a distinct meaning. To develop a more effective solution, we propose building a dataset that includes ambiguous acronyms found in various domains, along with their definitions and the emotions associated with them. Since standard evaluation metrics are not suitable for assessing acronym understanding, we also present a method for evaluating the accuracy of acronym definitions. By incorporating both manual annotation and the benefits of machine learning, we demonstrate that the most reliable results are obtained by combining the two approaches. The study reveals that, when using a dataset with clear definitions, models can achieve nearly 100% accuracy; however, when encountering ambiguous acronyms for the first time, the models perform poorly, at approximately 40%. To address this issue, we propose a technique that leverages context and existing knowledge to disambiguate acronyms. The method proposed achieves the best overall results and outperforms models that rely on simple baseline evaluations. The study's findings highlight the importance of addressing ambiguous language and the need for more effective machine learning models that can handle novel situations. The proposed method and dataset are available for download. In conclusion, we have successfully demonstrated a method for identifying and disambiguating acronyms in various writing domains with good results, and we believe this study lays the groundwork for further research in this area. In addition, we have obtained promising outcomes when testing the method on two distinct datasets containing ambiguous acronyms. The proposed approach has shown the greatest accuracy among the machine learning models evaluated and has achieved exceptional results when applied to two different datasets containing ambiguous acronyms. The study's findings are particularly significant because they address a significant issue affecting machine learning models and natural language processing systems - the handling of ambiguous language. The proposed method has several key advantages over other approaches, including the ability to operate independently of pre-defined dictionaries and to effectively employ both manual annotation and machine learning

Determining the density of neutrons in the central region of atomic nuclei, specifically the density difference between neutrons and protons, is a key objective of ongoing nuclear research. This goal is crucial in understanding how the strong interaction affects the distribution of nucleons within the nucleus. By participating in the Strong Interaction, the neutron skin thickness is directly linked to the symmetry potential as well as the effective mass of nucleons, which in turn influences the properties of dense nuclear matter found in neutron stars. In this study, we examine the relationship between the neutron skin thickness and the in-flight electroproduction of atomic nuclei at various energies, specifically using the JLab 12 GeV beam to measure the thickness of 140 atoms, such as oxygen, carbon, and aluminum, through measurement of the elastic scattering of electrons off these targets. By analyzing these measurements, we find that the calculated values of the neutron skin thickness are directly proportional to the effective mass of neutrons and the symmetry potential, which is derived from theoretical calculations of nuclear density distributions, and demonstrate that a significant advancement in the understanding of nuclear properties can be achieved through these measurements, which will also have a notable impact on the interpretation of future density functional theory calculations. Additionally, we anticipate that precise measurements of neutron skin thickness will become feasible with the arrival of the 10-20 GeV class of lepton beams, allowing for investigations of new phenomena in nuclear physics. If such a high-energy beam becomes available at the future upgrade of the Relativistic Heavy Ion Facility (RHIC), specifically with 10-20 GeV electrons or muons, it is possible to study the neutron skin thickness in various atomic nuclei, including stable and radioactive nuclei, by carrying out electrodisintegration experiments. These experiments have the potential to reveal more precise information about the density distributions of these nuclei and provide valuable insights into the properties of nuclear matter. Moreover, they could provide a stronger link between theoretical models of nuclear density functions and density distributions, and could also provide a crucial framework for understanding the behavior of nuclear matter in neutron stars. This research introduces the principal component geostatistical approach (PCGA) to approximate riverbed height based on measurements of flow velocity and direction, and develops a novel inverse problem framework that incorporates a detailed geostatistical model. Although invasive methods exist for measuring riverbed depth, they are costly and time-consuming, so there is a need for a more efficient solution. A numerical study was conducted where PCGA was pitted against traditional methods, such as the smooth stream function approach, in a hypothetical river with a complex bedrock landscape. Results showed that PCGA and traditional methods produced similar estimates of riverbed height, but PCGA required significantly fewer flow velocity measurements (twenty vs. hundred) to reach the same level of accuracy. Notably, PCGA was more robust to variations in flow velocity measurements, such as changes in measurement depth and spacing. The study demonstrated that PCGA offers a non-invasive, efficient, and robust method for estimating riverbed height using flow velocity measurements. The code developed in this research is openly available for public use.

Creating HDR images with a high dynamic range through exposure setting selection requires considering several factors including the quantity and quality of captured images. While research has been focused on developing optimization techniques, little attention has been given to designing automatic exposure setting selection algorithms. In response, this paper outlines the benefits of integrating machine learning into this process, showcasing the potential for superior HDR image quality. To support this goal, the paper presents two novel deep learning approaches, leveraging convolutional neural networks to directly produce high-quality HDR images from single images. The proposed methods, characterized by unsupervised and self-supervised training modes, offer enhanced HDR image creation capabilities, demonstrating significant improvements over existing methods and on par with state-of-the-art advanced algorithms requiring pairs of images. The proposed techniques also offer several advantages, including minimal training requirements and the ability to handle complex scenes. Comprehensive testing across various datasets confirms the superiority of the proposed methods over existing approaches, while further enhancing the potential for future research in this domain. The proposed algorithms are freely accessible at https://github.com/zyang12/AutoExposure.

Causal deep learning, an emerging field that integrates concepts from causal analysis and machine learning, has been widely adopted in recent statistics and ML research. However, the diverse range of methods within causal deep learning complicates efforts to identify existing research gaps. To provide a clearer overview, we categorize existing causal deep learning methods into three distinct categories - those that leverage identification conditions, those that use causal graphs, and those that are based on causal models - and review the key characteristics of each category. Additionally, we discuss existing challenges, potential solutions, and future directions for the field, including how to enhance the interpretability of causal deep learning methods and facilitate the widespread adoption of these methods in real-world applications.

The long-term temperature measurement in nuclear reactors relies on the use of radioactive cerium markers left over from the beginning of their operation. These markers continue to provide valuable information through in-core flux and power distribution measurements, neutron flux and power monitoring, and fission chamber temperature measurements. The most effective method involves comparing in situ measurements of proton resonance shifts in cerium nuclei as they return to equilibrium with the cooling reactor. The success of this approach requires accurate modeling of the proton resonance shift recovery process. While this model has been validated for certain conditions in the past, there were significant gaps in its theoretical foundation. The aim of this study is to fill these gaps through Monte Carlo simulations, by exploring the influence of neutron flux, power, and temperature on the cerium markers' radioactive decay, nuclear transmutations, and the resulting proton resonance shift recovery process. The research has demonstrated that the model can be a powerful tool for interpreting the experimental data obtained from in-core measurements, and has the potential to be incorporated into reactor performance assessment and safety management systems. The most notable advantage of this approach lies in its ability to provide highly accurate temperature measurements across various reactor channels, offering a significant improvement over the conventional method of temperature estimation. The study has also proven that the proton resonance frequency shift vs. temperature relationship can be accurately modeled using a polynomial function, and has validated the theoretical foundation of the Monte Carlo code by comparing the simulated data with independent measurements. The most interesting outcome of this research has been the discovery that the proton resonance frequency shift contributes to the temperature measurement error in a manner consistent with the total energy spectrum of the reactor, and has identified the key factors that influence the response of the reactor's energy spectrum to changes in power and location. The research has further demonstrated that the reaction time of the proton resonance frequency shift is essentially instantaneous, and has validated the theoretical foundation of the neutron flux and power monitoring method. The study has also demonstrated the potential to provide valuable additional information, including the detection of hidden faults, determination of the reactor's dynamic behavior, and selection of the optimal power operating point. The potential of the in-core measurements to provide this valuable additional information could provide a strong basis for the implementation of the in-core flux and power distribution measurement method in commercial nuclear reactors. The research has a significant bearing on the ongoing efforts to develop and implement in-core neutron noise analysis and machine learning methods in commercial nuclear reactors. The study has a further educational value, given the opportunity it provides for students and young researchers to gain hands-on experience of the development and implementation of reactor performance assessment

This study investigates how the Balancing Domain Decomposition by Constraints (BDDC) method's performance is influenced by the number of degrees of freedom on each subdomain, the number of BDDC constraints, and the problem's diffusion coefficient in a finite difference setting for an anisotropic elliptic problem. A specific focus is on understanding how these factors affect the BDDC's convergence and order of accuracy when solving systems resulting from a finite difference discretization of a constant coefficient elliptic equation. To analyze this, a simplified approach is taken that characterizes the BDDC's performance through its dependence on relative subdomain sizes, the number of degrees of freedom within subdomains, and the BDDC constraint count. Additionally, numerical experiments validate the obtained analytical predictions and examine the BDDC's performance in a varying anisotropic environment. The findings suggest that as subdomains become increasingly irregular in size, the BDDC's performance may degrade, but this negative effect can be mitigated through the use of more refined subdomain meshes without compromising the method's efficiency. The research also reveals that when solving systems of significant dimension, the BDDC's performance can be optimized by allocating more degrees of freedom to individual subdomains, given that this is feasible within the constraints of the given problem and implementation. The presented study provides valuable insights into the performance of anisotropic BDDC preconditioners and offers practical guidance for the effective application of this method to similar complex systems. The research is further supported by detailed numerical experiments examining how different anisotropic coefficient values impact the BDDC's performance. The findings from this study have significant implications for extending the anisotropic BDDC method to more general linear elliptic problems. Our comprehensive analysis provides a clear visual representation of these metrics in relation to time and a measure of variability, thereby illuminating complex phenomena such as correlated diffusion, heterogeneity, and the interplay between them. Lastly, we propose the concept of multi-dimensional time-averaged mean squared displacement spectra as a tool for comparing the relative influence of correlated motion, variations, and time across different systems. Through this proposal, we facilitate a more comprehensive discussion across related research fields.

We have developed a predictive framework for identifying unexpected fluctuations in population sizes within an ecological web by analyzing and simplifying a nonlinear model that reflects the interactions among populations. This model, based on a theory by May and Leonard, represents the complex relationships among populations using a linear regression model, which identifies the influence of specific conditions on the prevalence of sudden fluctuations in population sizes. Furthermore, we established a condition for the occurrence of sudden shifts in population sizes and a measure of the width of tails in those populations. We also investigated the relationship between this model and another well-known ecological model, based on Lotka-Volterra equations, and demonstrated that our framework applies to systems characterized by coexistence and stability. To illustrate our framework, we analyzed a dataset of lake trophic webs and used cross-validation to evaluate its performance. The model was able to effectively predict sudden fluctuations in population sizes in various instances and failed to do so in situations where local stability was an adequate predictor of fluctuations. Our framework is now available online through an interactive web tool that enables users to upload their own data and observe the predicted outcomes. The underlying code is also open to public use. The predictive model, along with the web tool, can be found at https://datascience.toro.com/web-base-ideal-free-zero.html. The code that generates the web app is hosted at https://github.com/usdt-data-science/web-ideal-free-zero. The dataset used in this study is presented in the accompanying file. The concept of ideal free theory provides a useful framework for understanding the relationships among populations within ecological webs, and our model offers a condition that can be applied to predict sudden fluctuations in population sizes, ultimately contributing to a better comprehension of the complex interactions within these ecosystems. The model we proposed can also facilitate discussions among ecologists, mathematicians, and statisticians working on the dynamics of population sizes. The condition we established, particularly the width of tails, offers a manageably simple statistical measure that is amenable to verification or falsification through existing data, thus representing a significant advancement in the field. The relationship between our model and another well-known ecological model has not been explored before, and our analysis of the dataset of lake trophic webs using cross-validation has a methodological value in itself. Transfer learning has significantly enhanced AI-based sentiment analysis, enabling it to be applied to many languages. Yet, even with significant accuracy in the source language, there is often a gap in efficacy in the target language. Our research aims to bridge this linguistic divide by employing a mixed-data training approach for a pre-trained BERT model. We employed a novel technique known as token-level label propagation to successfully enlist the aid of labeled data from the target language, thereby enhancing the BERT model's performance. Experimental findings with a dataset of customer reviews in Chinese and English demonstrate that this approach surpasses conventional domain adaptation methods, facilitating accurate sentiment analysis in the target language with limited labeled target-language data. Moreover, an analysis of the model's components, enabled by a technique called feature importance, provided valuable insights into the behaviors observed during the mixed-data training process. Our innovative approach has the potential to guide other methods for adapting pre-trained neural language models to multiple languages. Additionally, our research offers a valuable set of resources, including the code and trained models, to facilitate the development of more advanced sentiment analysis techniques in multiple languages.

Building on earlier work of Polymath and (to a lesser extent) Goldstein and Terence Tao, this article examines a conjecture of Terence Tao from 2019, which posits that virtually every nontrivial subset of integers contains a pattern of m consecutive elements within an arithmetic progression of length at least c(m) times m, where the gap between elements is between 1 and m. To further investigate this conjecture, the article considers a more limited scenario in which a subset of integers, when multiplied together in pairs, produces a sum that belongs to a specific quadratic form, specifically one that represents an arithmetic progression. The article demonstrates that under these conditions, there will always be a consecutive block of length greater than 2 (or any fixed number) within the subset, where the elements' sums produce numbers within the specified quadratic form. The article also explores related conjectures and provides a more detailed analysis of the required projective width in relation to conjugate quadratic forms. The article's findings regarding the conjugate of the form $x^2 + y^2$ lead to a broader discussion on the significance of this type of problem in number theory. The article's technique for dealing with complex conjugate fields also involves a discussion on how to apply Hilbert's criterion for reciprocity laws. The article's largest contribution is a more precise definition of the term 'virtual' in the context of sets of integers, as well as an exploration of its implications. Using the semiclassical imaginary time method, we calculate mixed semiclassical states for a chaotic Hénon-Heiles system. These calculations are carried out in an area-constrained condition, allowing us to compare both regular and chaotic state projections onto a chaotic potential surface. This comparison reveals that high-energy chaotic states in this system exhibit unique characteristics, with distributions that mimic those found in Gaussian states, with distinct scalings for their spread and energy consumption. Notably, our results contradict initial predictions suggesting increased classical action localization in chaotic regions, with our findings instead indicating a tendency toward localization within regular islands and the spread of energy across the entire available phase space in chaotic contexts. This phenomenon is further confirmed by our analysis of classical motion trajectories, where we observe Melnikov's test for chaos and find corresponding evidence of complex dynamics. Additionally, our study demonstrates the efficacy of Wigner function calculations in complex phase space, with implications for the study of other complex systems. Lastly, we propose that the phenomenon of increased energy spread in chaotic contexts may be an intrinsic feature of chaotic systems across the semiclassical regime.

Recently, high-performance models have achieved outstanding results in Visual Relationship Detection (VRD). Nonetheless, these models require substantial training data and exert significant pressure on memory resources. To overcome these challenges, we've developed a novel training approach called Balanced Negative Proposal Sampling (BNPS). This approach involves selectively presenting relationship proposals to the model with varying levels of negativity, aiming to counterbalance the inherent bias towards easy proposals. By incorporating BNPS, our experiments demonstrate notable enhancements in memory efficiency, model performance, and generalization ability. Moreover, BNPS can be seamlessly integrated into existing VRD models and represents a universally applicable solution. The code and data used in our research are now available for download.

Human motion prediction is a challenging task that is not fully resolved, even after significant advances in machine learning. A fundamental issue in addressing this challenge lies in acquiring sufficient quantities of high-quality training data, especially for the few-shot learning scenario. In this study, we examine supervised action recognition and prediction within the context of a data scarcity scenario. We test various models, including neural network-based architectures, utilising datasets of varying sizes, including extremely small datasets of just one example per class. Our findings indicate that robust models can be developed even in the absence of extensive training datasets, as demonstrated by our experiments employing the PyTorch framework. Our study aims to provide initial theoretical formulations and empirical validation for the error rates observed in this scenario, based on our experiments utilizing the Karsoli dataset. The outcomes of our research have significant implications for the development of more effective model learning algorithms that can excel in scenarios with limited training data. Our study is accessible via the arXiv platform.

This paper describes the implementation of the Oregon Trail Content Addressable Parallel Processor, a custom-built content-addressable memory system built by the Educational Computing Center at the University of Oregon.  The Content Addressable Parallel Processor is comprised of up to 4096 individual memory cells, and is capable of complex operations including addition, subtraction, and bitwise OR, in addition to searching for specific data.  The system is connected to a host computer via a direct memory access controller, and is capable of independent operation in order to minimize interference with other programs.  Despite being a relatively basic system, the Content Addressable Parallel Processor has a wide range of applications, and is particularly suited to solving problems that involve large amounts of data and require a significant amount of processing power.  In addition to a detailed description of the system's architecture and functionality, this paper includes specific examples and performance data obtained through actual use of the Content Addressable Parallel Processor.  It also provides a perspective on the educational value of building and programming this type of system.  Finally, the source code and data for several programs that were run on the Content Addressable Parallel Processor are included in order to provide further insight into the system's capabilities.  In order to make the most effective use of this paper, the reader is expected to have a basic understanding of computer architecture and programming principles.  In addition, the inclusion of assembly language source code written for a specific type of computer may be of limited interest to readers outside of the computing community.  However, the issues and concepts explored in this paper are relevant to a wide range of special-purpose digital computers, and are therefore of interest to researchers and educators in the field of computer science.  In particular, the description and analysis of various content-addressable memory systems can provide valuable insights to professionals working in the field of computer science, in addition to students of computer science who are looking for a practical application of complex computer concepts.  In this paper, the Oregon Trail Content Addressable Parallel Processor is used as a real-world example of a complex computer concept, in this case specifically addressing issues related to interconnection networks, in order to illustrate the complex computer concepts of multiple communication paths, independent operation, and interference reduction through prioritization.  The performance of the Content Addressable Parallel Processor has been measured and compared to alternative solutions that utilize regular memory, in the form of programs that calculate the sum of large numbers of random memory cells, determine the minimum value among large numbers of random memory cells, and locate specific data within large memory arrays. About 50% of bugs in software could be addressed through the use of partial and inconsistent information about the program's behavior. Our research aims to investigate a novel approach that leverages neural programs as the fundamental unit of program analysis and understanding. We propose a method to generate neural programs through a combination of static program analysis and learning from limited data, with the goal of improving this process by incorporating weak supervision from analysis tools embedded within the program itself. Our method involves using a type of neural network that can generate code in a program-in-the-wild context, with the goal of producing programs that accurately reflect the program's actual behavior and are free from common errors. We demonstrate through a language-based bug-finding application that program analysis knowledge acquired from limited data can be significantly enhanced, with the program understanding improved by nearly 50% through the neural program alone, and almost 90% with the aid of weakly-supervised learning. This approach also offers several benefits, including the ability to easily integrate new analysis features and have access to advanced program understanding capabilities that would be difficult to achieve through traditional methods. Moreover, our method allows bug reports with no explicit specification of the affected program section to be addressed, with results showing a success rate of over 70%. This has tangible implications for the development of program analysis tools and could potentially pave the way for the use of neural programs in other applications involving the analysis of software and databases. We also introduce a new language called Pyjs, a JavaScript-like language, with the purpose of testing and validating our approach. We believe our research opens up new avenues for exploring the relationship between program understanding and program specification, and is thus worthy of further investigation. We have made our code and data set available online.

Deep learning techniques have significantly elevated anomaly detection capabilities, especially when supported by vast amounts of labeled data. Yet, many real-world applications involve scale extensions where new data arrives continuously, making existing methods impractically limited. To address this challenge, we've developed an incremental anomaly detection framework based on a dual-learning approach. This framework uses a primary model for initial anomaly detection and a secondary model for correcting and refining its findings on expanded datasets. By implementing data augmentation and a decision-based technique to handle code mismatch, our approach achieves heightened accuracy across data phases. Experimental validations conducted on four public datasets demonstrate performance enhancements over top anomaly detection methods and incremental learning benchmarks, as well as in-depth analysis into our approach's effectiveness. A cryptographic scheme has a significant shortcoming if it enables an authority to force a user to reverse an encryption, even when the encryption can be faked. This issue becomes a critical concern if the encryption is part of a digital currency system. Our research demonstrates that, unless specific conditions are met, the government can compel a user to decrypt information, given that the encryption can be made to appear as though it originated from another individual. This problem persists even if the encryption is part of a digital currency system, unless additional properties are present, such as transaction visibility, to prevent the authority from learning sensitive information, thereby protecting the user's anonymity. Building upon existing work, we develop a particular type of homomorphic encryption based on the ELWE scheme, addressing this complication, and, in doing so, establish a key exchange protocol and a digital currency system with anonymity preservation. Furthermore, we showcase the feasibility of our approach through a practical implementation, incorporating a programming language tool to create an efficient compiler for homomorphic operations. This implementation demonstrates the potential of elusory encryption to serve as a viable solution for sensitive data applications, such as financial transactions, with minimal performance loss. Our approach achieves this without relying on costly multilinear maps, fully homomorphic encryption, or other resource-intensive constructions. Instead, we employ an integrated approach, combining an efficient underling encryption scheme, a key exchange protocol based on the user's encryption policy, and a compiler for a particular programming language, ensuring both security and efficiency in practice. This research provides an elusory encryption approach that offers an acceptable balance between security, efficiency, and usability, which is a crucial consideration for any cryptographic technology if it is to be adopted by the public. As such, elusory encryption may now be considered a feasible solution for sensitive data applications, such as financial transactions, without incurring an undue performance loss. We examine various strong coherent light-matter interaction-based measurement-device-independent quantum key distribution protocols that employ reflected weak coherent pulses. A comprehensive analysis is conducted on three specific proposals, involving single-photon counting, click measurement statistics, and the interference between two weak coherent pulses. For each scenario, we develop relevant models describing the process and associated statistics. Furthermore, we develop a comprehensive framework for evaluating the performance of these protocols in terms of gain, error rate, and final key rate. This framework allows for a comparative analysis of the different protocols. We also investigate the impact of various system parameters, including the number of phases and the number of subcategories, on the protocol performance. Additionally, we investigate the impact of weak coherent pulses on the protocol performance. We demonstrate that one of the protocols, specifically the one involving click measurement statistics, yields the highest gain and key rate. We also find that increasing the number of phases and using a high baseline threshold can significantly improve the protocol performance. However, there are optimal values for the number of phases and the baseline threshold that maximize gain and key rate. We also find that the protocols requiring strong coherent light and vacuum states may have disadvantages, such as low gain and low key rate. We propose modifying the basic MDI-QKD protocol to address these issues. We present numerical simulations validating our analysis and demonstrating the potential effectiveness of the protocols, especially the one involving click measurement statistics. We believe our analysis and findings are valuable contributions to the development and assessment of strong coherent light-matter interaction-based MDI-QKD protocols.

This success is specifically limited to problem instances where the total value of satisfactory assignments exceeds a polynomially large threshold, specifically $\Delta^{2n}$ for $n$ variables and a set of constraints marked by $\Delta$. Furthermore, our PTAS methodology builds upon existing techniques for problems with specific properties, such as unsatisfiability and the presence of a large value for certain constraints. This paper focuses on developing high-order numerical techniques for solving a particular type of time-dependent mean field games system, which consists of a system of partial differential equations describing the evolution of two variables, $u$ and $v$. The challenge in achieving this goal lies in the presence of a term that is composed of the product of $u$ and $v$, which necessitates a novel application of an implicit-implicit method. By establishing an essential inequality and leveraging the concept of mesh independence, we can devise an implicit-implicit numerical scheme on a structured grid that guarantees convergence and attains the same order as its continuous counterpart. Moreover, we can enhance the scheme's performance by introducing a higher-order interpolation method, which enables us to achieve the same rate of accuracy while reducing the number of algebraic computations. Ultimately, we can achieve the desired order of accuracy while minimizing the computational cost through a higher-order interpolation method, which demonstrates a notable improvement in the solution's efficiency. This innovative approach paves the way for the efficient numerical solution of a range of time-dependent mean field games systems. System models described by similar systems of equations can also be solved using this approach, and we provide numerical demonstrations to verify its effectiveness. KIC 9267654 is a remarkable star that rotates in the opposite direction to the majority of similar A-type stars, which mostly rotate in the direction determined by the Galactic standard of motion. Instead, we propose that the star's unusual behavior could be attributed to its being part of a stellar group that interacts strongly, such as an association or a moving group, or perhaps it is an isolated star with a unique history. To better understand the stellar properties of KIC 9267654, we conducted a detailed analysis, using spectroscopic and photometric data to refine its parameters. Identifying and countering the spread of false information is becoming increasingly vital in today's information age. Social media platforms are exploring methods to detect and prevent the dissemination of fake news, but their approaches are hampered by data privacy constraints and the need for substantially more effective detection models. This study introduces MetaFEND, a groundbreaking, open-source fake news detection framework that leverages meta-learning and incorporates multiple perspectives to significantly improve the accuracy of false information detection. Unlike conventional models that rely on static features and struggle to cope with language evolution, MetaFEND utilizes a dynamic approach to capture the permanent and temporary characteristics of language. This is achieved by employing a multi-head perspective-taking mechanism that combines the model's internal representations with those of peer models trained on diverse datasets. Furthermore, the incorporation of a opposing decoder helps to enhance the accuracy by comparing predicted outputs with those of a fake news generator. Experimental results show that MetaFEND significantly outperforms existing models, surpassing RoBERTa by up to 13% in F1 score and 7% in label bias, while successfully mitigating big bias up to 41 points. The framework's effectiveness in modeling permanent and temporary language characteristics is highlighted by the implementation of an evolutionary algorithm that adapts MetaFEND to new tasks with minimal labeling. This paper compares the average age of information (AoI) in discrete and continuous time systems that maintain update histories and always know the current time. We model a discrete time system that updates its values at integer time points and obtain an infinite discrete time series for the AoI distribution. In contrast, a continuous time system generates an ongoing, non-stationary age distribution following each new update. We establish a relationship between the two age distributions and demonstrate that their stationary components are identical, while the non-stationary component in the continuous time system arises from the summation of all stationary sub-distributions. Furthermore, we analyze two models where updates are generated in integer time increments: one with a fixed update period and the other with an arbitrarily distributed period. We derive the AoI distribution in the first model and the sum of its stationary sub-distributions in the second model. We validate our theoretical findings by conducting simulations and presenting corresponding results. Additionally, we investigate how the average AoI is affected by update intervals both theoretically and through Monte Carlo methods. We also establish that the discrete time system's AoI performance surpasses that of the continuous time system due to its stationary age components and the beneficial effects of time increments on AoI growth. We then employ our results to inform the design of random generators and discuss potential applications in science and engineering. Lastly, we outline potential future directions for research in AoI metrics and related fields. These future directions involve extending our research to accommodate time-varying systems, exploring new optimization approaches, and investigating the statistical properties of AoI distributions. We investigated the influence of the lattice structure and dopants on the Heisenberg spin exchange interaction in a silicon crystal lattice. Our analysis revealed that the exchange interaction can be either ferromagnetic or antiferromagnetic depending on the location of the spins within the lattice. Notably, the shape of the exchange interaction's profile along specific crystallographic directions can be modified to favor a particular spin alignment (ferromagnetic or antiferromagnetic) over another through careful placement of the spins in a silicon matrix. In fact, introducing a non-magnetic impurity at specific locations can also switch the type of spin alignment preferred. Our findings also indicated that the exchange interaction's magnitude can be adjusted through the placement of a magnetic impurity, with examples shown for substitutional and interstitial sites. We observed the largest enhancement of the exchange interaction's magnitude when the magnetic impurities were located at the silicon sites adjacent to a vacancy, where the exchange interaction's magnitude was over 100 times greater than the sum of the individual impurities' contributions. These results offer promising avenues for manipulating exchange interaction in silicon crystal lattices and may have significant implications for the development of quantum technologies.

Specifically, in situations where an unextendible product base (UPB) is present, the system displays strong quantum nonlocality. We have newly identified two sets of three-qutrit UPB systems that exhibit this property. Additionally, we have proven that these two sets are the only such collections, making our findings comprehensive. Prior to this discovery, only one set of parameters describing a scenario of this type was known. Our discovery more than quadruples the number of such scenarios documented to date. We have also analytically demonstrated the connection between the entanglement swapping process and the strong quantum nonlocality present in these systems, utilizing a process known as Simon's process. This new approach yields a significant improvement in efficiency when comparing to prior methods. We have also established that this new method has a high success rate in producing UPB collections, especially when the system's rank is higher. Prior methods were found to be more effective for systems of lower rank. Astrobot navigation must balance two objectives: ensuring the safety of its movements to avoid collisions with other astrobots, and optimizing its trajectory to minimize disruptions and prevent interference. Nevertheless, the rise in survey sizes leads to computing time explosions for traditional algorithms, rendering them impractical for large-scale scenarios. In response, we present a new trajectory planning algorithm that leverages geometric programming and multi-level decomposition to divide complex problems into more manageable pieces, allowing for faster solution times without sacrificing precision. In conjunction with a new astrobot trajectory safety protocol, this algorithm ensures that all astrobots can coexist peacefully and efficiently gather data from their assigned targets during the survey. When tested against the current standard algorithm, our method yields substantial enhancements in processing speed while still maintaining equal levels of performance. Specifically, when examining medium-sized surveys, our algorithm outperforms the competitor by an average of 35-fold, while large surveys see an even more substantial gain of nearly 500 times. As such, this new algorithm is an ideal solution for the complex astrobot navigation challenges posed by massive spectroscopic surveys. In addition, our method opens up new avenues for further study and optimization in this domain. Recent advancements in natural language processing have focused on utilizing knowledge graph triples as pseudo-text for pre-training. Contrary to conventional text-based pre-training, this knowledge-based approach often lacks evaluation of the underlying data's factual accuracy. In our research, we examine whether utilizing faulty knowledge triples for pre-training leads to similar performance gains as seen in regular text-based pre-training. To achieve this, we present two types of faulty knowledge triples: (1) falsely attributed triples (e.g., "Albert Einstein was born in Krakow") and (2) incomplete or unclear triples (e.g., "The main hormone producing part of the adrenal gland"). We compare models pre-trained with these faulty knowledge triples to those pre-trained with accurate knowledge triples and find they perform similarly. Furthermore, we discover that utilizing traditional text-based pre-training yields better question-answering results than the knowledge-based approach. Nonetheless, our research also reveals that specific models benefit from knowledge-based pre-training, particularly when confronted with questions containing entities previously encountered during knowledge-based pre-training. This implies that knowledge-based pre-training can offer complementary advantages. We also examine the knowledge retrieval aspect and find that utilizing faulty knowledge triples leads to retrieved triples being more diverse, which in turn enhances question-answering performance. Ultimately, our findings suggest that knowledge-based pre-training's performance gains result from both improved language modeling and enhanced knowledge retrieval, and as such, it represents a promising direction for future research. This study examines how classical partial differential equation (PDE) models are approximated by nonlocal diffusion models as their interaction kernels shift from nonlocal to local behavior. We investigate both stationary and time-dependent nonlocal PDEs, focusing on kernels that take on local character as they are confined to smaller ranges, similar to how Gaussian kernels behave with decreasing standard deviations. We demonstrate that these classical and nonlocal models have comparable solutions, with the nonlocal models providing a meaningful interpretation of boundary values as the kernel's range shrinks, thus accurately capturing the underlying boundary conditions. This understanding is further validated through numerical experiments. Notably, we show that nonlocal models can be viewed as relaxing classical boundary conditions under regularization, with the effect being particularly visible in models defined on domains with irregular shapes. It is also evident that approximating classical PDEs with nonlocal models offers a regularizing effect on solutions with rough boundary values. As a result, we can obtain smooth solutions for nonlocal models, despite the solution's rough nature being inherent to the corresponding classical PDE. This phenomenon is illustrated through a nonlocal Stefan problem. We then devise a numerical method based on the implicit Euler scheme and operator splitting, with the purpose of approximating the nonlocal in time. The proposed method is numerically verified to accurately capture the nonlocal model's behavior, especially its local-to-classical limit as the kernel's range diminishes. The method is also applied to solve a nonlocal Stefan problem, with the results demonstrating its capability to reproduce the classical model's solution patterns, further highlighting the nonlocal model's role in mitigating rough solutions through its regularizing effect. The implementation of the method is made publicly available as part of the ALBERT library. We expect this work to provide a foundation for further investigation into the local-to-classical limit of nonlocal models, especially in relation to models defined on irregular domains. As such, we encourage contributions to the ongoing research in this area. These applications often incorporate Inertial Measurement Units (IMUs) for their accuracy and low cost. Our research builds upon existing work that uses IMUs with computer vision technology to capture panoramic images. We tested various capture methods, including both two-dimensional feature-based and machine learning approaches, for stitching images. Our evaluation revealed that a method incorporating IMU data and the Direct Sparse Visual Odometry algorithm yielded superior results. Specifically, it produced higher mesh quality and more accurate point clouds, as measured by mesh complexity and precision. To further enhance performance, we incorporated two optimization techniques, tailoring capture angles to minimize gaps between consecutive images. Implementing these strategies, we optimized capture angles dynamically. Our findings demonstrated notable improvements in mesh complexity (by 2.5-fold) and precision (within 1.5-fold), as well as reduced stitching processing time (by 2.7-fold). We validated our approach by capturing and stitching images in real-world scenarios with promising results. Our approach has the added benefit of minimizing data collection during initial setup, lowering the need for precise calibration. This paper builds on work initiated in arXiv:2012.04835, further exploring the spectrum of degenerate Eisenstein series on the group $G=SO_4($Q_(o)$)$. Specifically, it identifies and analyzes the holomorphic representations within this spectrum, drawing on the underlying geometry of Weyl group cosets. Consequently, the paper establishes a precise description of the representations in question, drawing on earlier findings regarding the dual action of the Weyl group and a key isomorphism from the Weyl group to the Galois group. Moreover, it derives explicit formulas governing the rates of growth for certain L^2 norms associated with these representations. This research ultimately provides a more comprehensive understanding of the spectrum of degenerate Eisenstein series on $G=SO_4($Q_(o)$)$. Crucially, it demonstrates the pivotal role played by the geometry of Weyl group cosets in this analysis. Additionally, it implies key consequences for the study of automorphic L-functions within this context. Lastly, it highlights the potential for further generalizations beyond the $SO_4($Q_(o)$)$ case.

A Convolution Recurrent Network (CRN) model has been successful in speech enhancement, but it falls short due to its limited scope in the time-frequency domain. This limitation is addressed by the proposed Dual-Path Convolution Recurrent Network (DPCRN), which adds a dual-path mechanism that enables the model to capture local and global dependencies in the time-frequency domain. By incorporating dual-path convolutions and making use of the frequency axis, DPCRN outperforms the conventional CRN model by improving speech quality and reducing over-smoothing in hidden layers. Experimental results show that DPCRN achieves superior performance compared to CRN and other speech enhancement networks in both subjective and objective evaluations, with data from the LJS1 and VCTK datasets. Additionally, DPCRN is shown to have a higher capacity than CRN but with less over-smoothing, as evidenced by its frequency-scale dilated convolution architecture. This implies that DPCRN is an efficient model with higher performance. Moreover, DPCRN improves speech quality without introducing noise in clean speech samples, as shown in comparative output spectra.
