Automatically interpreting scanned documents containing pre-printed text and various forms of handwriting is a challenging task. The interpretation becomes even more difficult when the handwriting does not follow the original text structure. The widespread adoption of pre-trained language models in document interpretation is hindered by their limited ability to accurately associate pre-printed and handwritten text. The issue is compounded by the presence of noisy images, which impairs the performance of both text recognition and relationship detection. To address this challenge, we propose Document Understanding via Iterative Reasoning (DIAR), an innovative approach that involves both iterative reasoning and a document understanding module. The core contribution of this work involves introducing a new iterative reasoning module, inspired by the global-average-pooling technique, that enhances the accuracy of relationship detection between pre-printed and handwritten text in noisy document images. The performance of DIAR is demonstrated by applying the approach to two diverse datasets, resulting in significant improvements over existing state-of-the-art approaches. The study also highlights the benefits of using a document understanding module in isolation, which surprisingly reveals that simply using this module alone achieves comparable performance to the entire DIAR system. Additionally, an examination of the proposed iterative reasoning module through attention analysis and degradation analysis confirms that this module successfully captures the underlying document structures and is critical for accurate relationship detection. The code and dataset are openly available at: https://github.com/whui5/Document-Understanding-via-Iterative-Reasoning. The work has been accepted for publication at the 2022 IEEE/ACM Conference on Connected Data for All (CDA).

This approach allows us to apply linear vector autoregressive models and conduct a comprehensive stability analysis, which can also be applied to standard complex networks. Our method enables the evaluation of the stability of multilayer networks by transforming the complex system into a simplified description and then analyzing the stability of the resulting standard complex networks. We illustrate our approach by investigating the stability of a multilayer network consisting of two interacting layers and derived from a susceptible-infected model. This is accompanied by an empirical analysis of the effectiveness of our method on synthetic and real-world datasets. Our approach can be employed in collaboration with contemporary stability analysis techniques to assess the stability of multilayer networks. Furthermore, our method facilitates the generation of active and passive surveillance strategies aimed at monitoring and managing multilayer networks. These strategies are generated in the form of a control policy that ensures the multilayer network transitions to a stable state, and can be applied to a broader class of network dynamics, including vector autoregressive models, autoregressive integrated moving average models, and nonlinear models that resemble the spread of disease. Roudeault recently introduced a new type of operator in the context of differential modules, specifically operators of the type $D_t = (D_s + M)(1 - \frac{1}{t}S_t)$, where $D_s$ and $D_t$ correspond to the differential operators associated with $s$ and $t$ respectively, $M$ is a matrix, and $S_t$ is the Teichmüller operator. It has been demonstrated that these operators $D_t$ are analytically continuing $D_s$ and they share the same eigenoperators as $D_s$. The paper expands on this concept by introducing operators of the form $D_t = (D_s + N)(1 - \frac{1}{t}T_t)$, where $T_t$ is an alternative representation of the Teichmüller operator, and it has been proven that under specific conditions, these operators $D_t$ analytically continue $D_s$. The paper additionally explores connections between these operators and Borel operators. It has been shown that certain operators of the type $D_t = (D_s + N)(1 - \frac{1}{t}T_t)$ can be viewed as limitations of Borel operators and they have the ability to analytically continue $D_s$. The paper also delves into the relationship between these operators and multiple zeta values, presenting specific examples of their application. A cutting-edge algorithm used in a testing environment can accurately detect and fix errors made during a simple text-based game development process.  As the program runs, the algorithm raises exceptions indicating possible flaws in the code, and a set of customized patch functions becomes active to rectify the issues.  The exceptions and patch functions are crafted to mirror the structure and content of the game's underlying data model, ensuring that the program is fixed in a way that makes sense in the context of the game.  We plan to present the outcomes of a user study involving three experienced programmers who tested the algorithm's performance under various conditions.  The study measured the program's error detection and correction rates as well as the difficulties encountered by the users in responding to the exceptions and applying the patch functions.  Additionally, we collected and analyzed feedback from the users through a brief questionnaire.  The presented data demonstrates the success of the algorithm in identifying and fixing errors, and reveals interesting insights into the challenges faced by the users in handling certain types of errors.  We also discuss possible directions for enhancing the program in the future by leveraging techniques associated with the field of formal verification.  The complete implementation of the algorithm and the game is available online, and we invite the public to test the program and provide feedback.  We intend to build upon this work by exploring ways to adapt the algorithm to detect and fix additional types of errors, and to incorporate additional interactive proof systems inspired by the "hint" feature in the game.  We hope that this project will serve as a model for educating students on the benefits of using interactive proof systems in programming exercises. In response, we propose HyperNetworks with adaptive neural network components that learn to apply prompt prompts efficiently. By leveraging an auxiliary network that learns prompt prompts in relation to input sentences, we successfully applied our approach to several NLP tasks while reducing memory needs. In this work, we establish a significant connection between the maximally long root $\alpha_l$ in root systems of types $A_l$ and $D_l$, and the simplex structure. Specifically, we demonstrate that $\alpha_l$ is $ Coxeter$-orthogonal to all other roots within the system. This distinctive property makes the system analogous to a set of reflections in a hyperbolic space of two dimensions, resulting in a relationship between the roots and a geometric structure. Consequently, we can effectively classify the roots through their projection onto the line generated by $\alpha_l$. Furthermore, we define a chronologic order among the roots and demonstrate its alignment with their dimensionality. Moreover, we can recursively construct the entire root system by adding new roots in a specific order. This innovative perspective on root systems enables us to derive results for algebraic groups and Lie superalgebras with simple representations. We also examine Dynkin diagrams and diagrams of extended root systems in a way that reflects the geometric relationship between the roots. This approach also allows us to present an infinite sequence of roots within the system, thereby generating an affine root system through a combination of these elements, rather than the conventional use of the Weyl group. Finally, we apply these findings to the adjoint representation of simple Lie superalgebras in our final chapter. 

This work is complemented by an appendix written by Pavel Tupper, who builds upon our research by employing our methods to analyze the extended root systems of type $G_2$. His study reveals a sequence of roots within the system and provides a distinct arrangement of the Dynkin diagrams. Moreover, he presents a novel approach to constructing the Weyl group through a combination of these elements, rather than the conventional use of the reflection axis. This research is further expanded upon in the context of Lie superalgebras. 

We believe that our innovative perspective on root systems, coupled with the distinct examples provided by Tupper, will prove valuable in better understanding the geometry of Lie superalgebras and their representation theory.

In recent years, synchrotron light sources have played a significant role in the rapid advancement of experimental techniques for materials science, allowing for in-depth characterization of materials through in situ and in operando experiments. These experiments range from probing materials' structural characteristics to studying chemical reactions and reactions within working devices. To build upon the discoveries made possible by synchrotron light sources, it's essential to maintain and expand their capabilities through a coordinated approach between light sources, universities, and national laboratories. This approach should prioritize strategic collaborations, allocate funds for user access, and direct them towards developing new experiments and techniques that leverage the unique features of these sources. Through this vision, we aim to guide the future of synchrotron light sources in the United States by highlighting key aspects, including their place within the broader materials science landscape, the importance of user facilities in the national research agenda, the structure and operation of the synchrotron community, the role of government funding, and the strategic directions for the next decade, centered on enhancing user access, expanding research into new fields, developing new experiments and techniques, securing long-term funding, and continuing collaboration among light sources, universities, and national laboratories. The outcome of these efforts will be essential in maintaining the position of U.S. synchrotron light sources at the forefront of global research in materials and solid-state sciences. The report also includes an overview of the community's structure and operations, followed by a roadmap for the future, which has been endorsed by the U.S. synchrotron community. The document is intended to foster open discussion within the community and with relevant funding agencies. The vision outlined herein will undergo regular review to ensure it aligns with the evolving needs of the community and the broader materials science landscape. We have derived a new formulation of the obstacle problem with variable coefficients, which implies a similar result for the original problem with constant coefficients when the obstacle meets a certain Sobolev regularity standard. Additionally, we have obtained an improvement for the original problem when the obstacle is more smoothly graded, specifically in two-dimensional space. Furthermore, we have investigated a related problem with non-normalized constraints and provided an alternative approach to solving it explicitly. This research was motivated by a goal of addressing similar issues in a different problem, the Serfaty--Rougerie Ginzburg-Landau type problem, which encompasses the obstacle problem as a sub-model. We have achieved our outcomes by combining both analysis-based and geometric approaches, the latter of which also offers a novel perspective on the underlying geometry of the obstacle. This perspective allows us to establish a significant consequence: a condition on the rate of change of the obstacle's volume is crucial in controlling the normal component of the curvature of the level sets of the solution. We have applied this understanding to obtain additional results, including both a qualitative description of the set where the solution achieves its minimum and an explicit solution to the related non-normalized problem. These outcomes have an independent significance in the context of the original problem, the Ginzburg-Landau type problem, and a related problem of Sharipov. They also imply new regularity properties for both the solution and its level sets in the presence of an irregular obstacle with finite energy. Lastly, our approach has yielded an interesting open question related to the minimality of the set where the solution achieves its minimum. This set has a non-trivial dimension and exhibits a unique structure; however, its minimal property appears to be a consequence of the specific symmetry of the obstacle rather than a general property of the solution. This observation suggests that further research is warranted to fully comprehend the geometric properties of the solution and its level sets. It also raises the question of whether similar phenomena exist in the absence of such high levels of symmetry. This question takes on additional significance in the context of the recent work of Delgadillo and Serrin on the regularity of partitions in another problem of this class. Quantum annealing is an optimization technique that relies on gentle transformations from a starting state to a ground state representing the solution to a given problem. This method involves two critical processes: diagonalization and decoherence. While diagonalization is concerned with identifying the ground state, decoherence affects the state during the annealing process. Investigating the impact of decoherence is essential to ensure the effectiveness of quantum annealing. This study simulates the application of quantum annealing to a classic problem, specifically the Ising model, and investigates how decoherence affects the success of reaching the target ground state. Our findings indicate that quantum annealing can be highly sensitive to decoherence, and in some instances, may fail to find the ground state due to decoherence. This failure can be attributed to the destruction of quantum coherence rather than the inability to identify the ground state. We also examine potential solutions to mitigate the influence of decoherence, including the use of kilizice annealing and quantum annealing with periodic resets. While these approaches show promising results in our simulations, further research is necessary to fully understand their potential in real-world applications. Additionally, we discuss the relationship between two-time and one-time protocols in quantum annealing, and our simulations suggest that the latter may offer improved resistance to decoherence. To demonstrate the practical feasibility of these protocols, we propose an implementation using an annealer based on coupled quantum spins, and show that kilizice annealing can be carried out using current technology. This study contributes to a deeper understanding of the interplay between quantum annealing, decoherence, and the two-time and one-time protocols, and provides valuable insights for the development of more resilient quantum annealing. This research also explores the feasibility of implementing kilizice annealing with periodic resets in real-world applications. In 1902, the Kapteyn Astronomical Laboratory was established in Groningen as a second national astronomical research institute, alongside the one in Leiden. Due to its location, the Groningen institute struggled to secure funding and contributions from local stakeholders. In contrast, the Leiden facility enjoyed significant support from the local community, reflecting the diverse cultural and economic circumstances prevalent in the Netherlands during that period. This study compares the environments, societies, and astronomical research conducted at the two institutions from their foundation in 1902 to 1999, accounting for their distinct developmental paths. Despite these differences, both the Kapteyn Astronomical Laboratory and the Leiden observatory were able to make notable contributions to various aspects of astronomical research, as evidenced by publications and awards given to their staff. In terms of employment, education, and management, the two institutions shared many similarities, ultimately leading to the merger of the Kapteyn Astronomical Laboratory into the Leiden observatory in 2000. This merged entity, known as the Leiden Institute of Physics, continues to operate within the university's physics department, with the Kapteyn Astronomical Laboratory being its research division. Our institution's remote learning model for undergraduate calculus and engineering modules revealed a significant disparity in module participation between under-represented minority students and their non-under-represented counterparts. To address this, we introduced an adapted participation scheme that incorporated oral presentation assessments in a hybrid in-person and online learning environment. Consequently, there was an increased presence of under-represented minority students in module activities and assessments, with their participation rates rising to comparable levels to their non-under-represented peers for certain modules, albeit still lagging in others. Notably, under-represented minority students' engagement in peer assessment partners shifted from none to a majority involvement. Post-module review feedback from both groups revealed satisfaction with the adapted scheme, citing an enhanced sense of responsibility and accountability among students to prepare for presentations. Nevertheless, some students from both groups expressed concerns about public speaking, which our institution aims to address through additional communication skills training within our engineering curriculum. The success of this approach has prompted our curriculum team to adopt these adapted participation strategies across multiple modules and is now being reviewed by our engineering department chairperson for widespread implementation. These identities are shown to correspond to the symmetry of the $A_2^{(1)}$ Virasoro algebra, explicitly displaying the closure. We confront this theory with the massive higher-spin conformal field theory in $d=3$, based on the $SU(3)$ Toda theory, by imposing periodic boundary conditions. We demonstrate that the Ward identities are satisfied and the closure of the higher-spin symmetry is confirmed. We also establish the relationship between the fields of the $SU(3)$ Toda conformal field theory and the massive higher-spin conformal field theory. These magnetic operators are shown to be related to the normalized trace operators of the massive higher-spin conformal field theory. We conclude that the $SU(3)$ Toda conformal field theory provides a theoretical framework for the massive higher-spin conformal field theory in $d=3$. We further establish that these magnetic operators serve as order parameters for the infinite tower of conserved high-spin currents in the $SU(3)$ Toda conformal field theory. High-frequency brain signals detected through electrocorticography (ECoG) have been found to contain significant information about walking-related activities in individuals with spinal cord injuries, as demonstrated by the work presented here. To evaluate the efficacy of ECoG signal processing in predicting the ability to walk compared to standard electroencephalography (EEG), we conducted a comparative study between the two methods. Our findings show that ECoG signals yield a 85% accurate prediction rate (>0.85) for walking functions, surpassing the 50% predicted by conventional EEG methods. Furthermore, our results indicate that ECoG signals facilitate the detection of walking-related neural networks in the brain. Additionally, we observed a distinct distribution of ECoG signal activity between walking and resting states and discovered evidence of frequency locking in the high-frequency bands when performing activities related to walking. Together, these findings provide new insights into the role of high-frequency brain signals in motor function and suggest the potential for further development of ECoG-based walking recovery therapies. Furthermore, we have introduced a new feature extraction technique called time-frequency correlation (TFC) that can be applied to other brain signal processing scenarios. We have also shown that machine learning models incorporating TFC techniques yield more accurate predictions of walking functions compared to conventional methods. Ultimately, our study demonstrates the feasibility of predicting walking abilities from ECoG signals and lays the groundwork for the development of novel, targeted brain recovery therapies. Additionally, our work highlights the advantages of using ECoG signals over conventional EEG methods in predicting walking functions and provides new features and processing techniques that can be applied to other motor function prediction scenarios. We explore how a specific type of highly connected subgraph within a right-angled Artin group's representation on a tree can serve as a distinguishing feature that separates the action from those of more limited types of groups. Our study reveals that such a subgraph's existence, along with a particular generating set, is sufficient to establish that the group's action on the tree is transient. This finding generalizes a previous result by Bestvester and Handelman, which addressed the same question but under the additional constraint of finite vertex valencies. Our subnormal subgraph property also finds connections to various concepts within the fields of group theory and graph theory. Additionally, we examine the relationship between a subgraph's connectivity and its ability to represent a class of Coxeter groups on trees. Our analysis also enables us to characterize which graph structures can arise from the action of a right-angled Artin group on a tree. This characterization is non-trivial only when the group's defining graph contains a subgraph that connects two disjoint components. Otherwise, such a graph would implicitly demonstrate the group's action on the tree as transient. Consequently, our theory offers a new framework for classifying right-angled Artin groups based on their fundamental graph properties rather than dynamic properties of their actions. This framework also provides a potential tool for analyzing group actions within a more general context. The development of population genetics research is closely tied to evolutionary theory and phylogeny reconstruction. Over time, analysts have employed a variety of methods to track the evolution of species, ranging from detailed simulations to tree-based models, all of which rely on stochastic processes. Despite the significance of these processes, many population genetics analyses have historically been non-stochastic, with the exception of simulations. The population size (N) is arguably the most crucial parameter in population genetics, with the greatest impact on how populations evolve and diversify. However, the population size has often been treated inaccurately or with no consideration at all in the literature. The purpose of this chapter is to clarify the population size's influence on the diversity of species and the evolution of traits through various stochastic processes in population genetics. The population size determines the rate of genetic drift, migration, mutation, and selection, as well as the central speed of diffusion on phylogeny, and the population size's effects are examined through a range of models, from demographic transitions to the evolution of the Y chromosome. The chapter also examines the population size's impact on the divergence of species and the emergence of genetic innovations due to stochastic processes. The population size's influence on the evolution of traits through selective processes is more complex, as it is shaped by the force and strength of selection, but the chapter looks at cases of selective processes, including the evolution of the Y chromosome and the molecular co-evolution of host and parasite. The chapter concludes with consideration of the population size's role in the ongoing evolutionary debate between "hard" and "soft" selection, and the implications of population sizes observed in nature for the evolution of traits through stochastic processes. The chapter aims to provide an authoritative overview of the population size's effects on the evolution of species and the divergence of genetic innovations due to stochastic processes, and will have value for researchers in evolutionary analysis, phylogeny reconstruction, and related fields. The chapter is written in a way that graduate students in biology and related fields can easily understand its content. The chapter is composed of two main sections, covering demographic transitions and selective processes, as well as additional topics, and includes a range of mathematical models and algorithms for analyzing population sizes. The chapter includes numerous figures and tables that illustrate the population size's effects on the evolution of species and the divergence of genetic innovations due to stochastic processes, and provides authoritative insights on the population size's role in evolutionary analysis and phylogeny reconstruction. The chapter is a key reference for any course covering population genetics research, and will have a lasting impact

This paper introduces a new statistical test to evaluate significant changes in complex networks, specifically within the network autoregressive model (NARX) framework. Existing literature has established the benefit of NARX models in analyzing multivariate time series datasets, but their NARX parameter estimation is challenging due to the issue of non-identifiable parameters. To address this problem, we propose a likelihood ratio test that utilizes alternative parameters with identifiable properties, thereby enabling us to conduct a precise hypothesis test. Through simulation studies, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed method in comparing it with other approaches, including one that utilizes an innovative network distance measure. Furthermore, we illustrate the practical application of our method through an empirical analysis of stock price index data, where we investigate the NARX model's ability to detect significant changes following an economic shock, specifically the 2008 Global Financial Crisis. The results from our study can provide valuable insights into understanding how multivariate financial time series datasets respond to significant events at a network level. The associated software and data are available online for replication purposes.

To better understand how cells change shape in response to forces within bundles of proteins, it's essential to study individual stress fibers in detail. We created a theoretical model that accounts for the mechanical properties and active contraction of a single stress fiber, incorporating filament bundling and the activity of motor proteins at both ends. Our analysis shows that the active contraction of a stress fiber is influenced by the turn-over of actin filaments and is characterized by a distinct point of instability. The behavior of the stress fiber is compared to a recent experiment involving the use of laser tweezers to manipulate microspheres that adhere to actin filaments and measure the resulting forces. Our model predicts that as the speed of turning over actin filaments increases, the point of instability will move further away from the adhesion point, consistent with observed data. However, our study also indicates that turning over actin filaments plays a significant role in stress fiber behavior. Furthermore, our findings suggest that stress fibers may not be capable of generating the high forces produced by cells during shape changes, implying that forces produced by multiple stress fibers are required to achieve this level of force. Additionally, our model indicates that the contraction of stress fibers could be responsible for promoting further stress fiber growth, such as through increased filament bundling or the attachment of adhesions to existing stress fibers. Lastly, our research indicates that stress fibers may be involved in initiating cell polarity by contributing to the formation of planar cell poles and the establishment of an axis of symmetry. Overall, our study provides a foundation for a stress fiber network model that can be used to investigate a range of cellular phenomena related to mechanical behavior and shape change. Nevertheless, there are several aspects that require further experimentation before they can be validated, such as how stress fibers are initiated and how they are regulated during network reorganization. Lastly, our model can also be expanded to consider stress fibers in a three-dimensional space. As such, it offers a valuable framework for future research aimed at understanding the complex mechanical behavior of cells through stress fibers. Ultimately, our theoretical stress fiber model can be employed in in silico experiments to inform and direct in vitro and in vivo experiments, as well as be integrated with other components of the cell membrane, such as adhesions and filaments, to develop a comprehensive stress fiber network model. This, in turn, can be used to investigate how stress fibers contribute to higher-order cellular organization and the development of cell shape and polarity. As such, our stress fiber model represents a significant step towards developing a cell shape mechanism

Quantum system measurement is an intricate process that significantly influences the capabilities of quantum sensing. Our analysis demonstrates that, in optimal quantum jump measurement, the estimated location can be as precise as achieved with continuous measurement, albeit at a precision that is bounded by the quantum limit set by the system's decay rate. Notably, this precision advantage can be realized even when the system is not on a stable path. Our approach goes beyond the traditional model, where the influence of the measurement is confined to a single qubit system. We expand our analysis to a complex system consisting of two interacting qubits, where the measurement is found to exhibit a dichotomy between continuous and quantum jump measurement, where the former falls short and the latter surpasses the quantum limit set by the decay rate of a single qubit system. Our study offers a new perspective on the measurement debate and provides a more comprehensive understanding of quantum sensing, where the full dynamics of the system, including all possible quantum states, can be exploited to enhance the precision of the measurement. This approach is applicable to any quantum system subject to decay or dissipation.

We investigated the potential performance gain of efficient value function estimates when tested on a larger sample size, specifically in the context of policy learning. The value function can be efficiently approximated using temporal difference (TD) control variates, and our study aimed to evaluate the benefits of leveraging multiple independent samples for online learning. We analyzed the performance of these efficient estimates in a matrix bandit model and found that increasing the testing sample size from 1 to N resulted in a $O(\sqrt{\log N}/\sqrt{n})$ error reduction, where n denotes the number of policy evaluations. Furthermore, we established an error bound of $O(\sqrt{\log n}/\sqrt{n})$ by assuming access to a virtual population based on the sampled expectations. The feasibility and performance of these efficient estimates were also validated through simulated and real-world experiments. The results demonstrated a notable performance gain, especially when the testing sample size was large, and highlighted the potential of online learning on multiple independent samples for online policy learning. We also introduced an alternative approach using a single sample per update step and derived an error bound of $O(1/\sqrt{n})$. The comparative analysis highlighted the trade-off between computational efficiency and performance gain. The code and data are available at https://github.com/hengryn/td-cv-efx. The paper has been accepted for publication in Journal of Machine Learning Research.

This paper examines the performance of binary and adaptive power control methods in a large, interfering wireless network, where multiple access and interference are considered. Interestingly, in regions with very low data rates, the performance of the coordinate-based method surpasses that of the binary power control method. Numerical simulations are also presented to validate the derived theoretical findings. Ultimately, this work provides new insights into the effectiveness of power control methods in high-interference wireless networks.

This study introduces a novel multiple-time-step integration algorithm (MTSA) for numerical simulations of complex flows with interacting particles. Typically, simulations of this type utilize separate time steps for fluid and particle updates; however, this can limit the integration step size due to Eulerian fluid resolution constraints. The proposed MTSA targets the efficient computation of such simulations by integrating the particle movement over multiple time steps, thus requiring fewer total time steps. As a result, the algorithm delivers a significant boost in computational speed, especially for large-scale, distributed simulations. To ensure accuracy, the particle position is corrected after each step, using a modified version of the successful quasi-constant acceleration method. The algorithm's performance is evaluated against a range of benchmarks, including an analysis of its error characteristics. The results demonstrate that MTSA possesses comparable precision to other methods, while providing a substantial increase in speed. The algorithm is subsequently implemented in a full-scale simulation of an airway model, involving the movement of thousands of particles, and is shown to produce an accurate and computationally efficient solution. This model goes beyond conventional methods that simply identify relationships within a network by utilizing a document hierarchy that reflects the network's structure. We have developed an efficient L1 sparse HDTM (L1SHDTM) algorithm to tackle the challenge of achieving model selection and feature extraction for HDTM. Our research utilizes data from Linux and Windows systems and demonstrates the efficacy of our methods in comparing system call sequences. Understanding the unique combination of magnetic and superconducting properties in nickelates requires analyzing the effects of substitution on the crystal and electronic structures. To delve into these effects, we use the Generalized Gradient Approximation + U technique to calculate the atomic and crystalline structures of Nd$_2$CuO$_4$ and Nd$_{0.82}$Sr$_{0.18}$CuO$_2$, then employ the Frozen Orbital Exact Momentum Broadening method to obtain the band structures and chemical potentials for both materials. Our study indicates that substitution enhances the mixing of Nd 4f states with the Cu 3d bands, especially around the Fermi level, and reveals the existence of back-doped states in the Lattice-Fermi-Gap of Nd$_{0.82}$Sr$_{0.18}$CuO$_2$. To further investigate these effects, we use the Downfolded 2-band model, and our results match experimental data. Notably, we find that substitution raises the Energy of the flat band and shifts the momentum of the peak within it. These changes facilitate the formation of a larger Fermi surface, more significant mixing between the Nd 4f and Cu 3d states, and ultimately, superconductivity in the system. Overall, our results highlight the importance of covalent effects in determining the electronic structures of nickelates and the need to consider multiple effects to achieve satisfactory agreement with experimental evidence. To facilitate ongoing discussion, we provide our calculated data in numerically convenient forms.

This paper investigates decay rates for solutions to the non-cutoff Boltzmann equation under weak uniform bounds on the initial data, specifically examining cases where the collision kernel has singularities of $|d|^{-\sigma}$ with $\sigma \in (0,1)$.  By analyzing the linearized equation, we establish upper and lower bounds for decay times of solutions in the Fourier space, characterized by $\sigma$-dependent values.  These results demonstrate that decay rates increase from exponential to polynomial as the singularity of the collision kernel increases from $\sigma=0$ to $\sigma=1$.  Additionally, we find that this transition occurs more rapidly for higher modes.  These findings counterbalance previous arguments that relied on estimates from the non-linear theory.  We further demonstrate that this more precise decay time-scale is comparable to, up to a logarithmic factor, the time required for the solutions to approach equilibrium.  This study is based on an enhanced analysis of the linearized Boltzmann equation, involving an explicit computation of the spectrum of the collision operator and a more precise examination of the decay of time-scales in a particular frequency parameterization.  This research has significant implications for the global-in-time existence theory of the full non-linear Boltzmann equation. This outcome has notable consequences for our understanding of the equilibrium phase transition in the Boltzmann equation. This research offers an alternative to the conventional Gaussian distribution used in the Bretschneider and Pierson-Moskowitz spectra models. The proposed biweibull model was verified using field data from severe storms in the North Atlantic during the 1998 cyclone Blake and the 2003 cyclone Jane, as well as data from the TOGA COBE (Tropical Ocean Global Atmosphere) experiment. The spread of infectious diseases like COVID-19 has escalated in recent times, causing widespread illness and death, as well as severe economic consequences. Public health crises of this magnitude necessitate early monitoring of infection rates, as well as timely intervention. Social media can serve as a valuable source of information for understanding public perceptions and emotions during a crisis, but it also poses the risk of spreading misinformation. In this paper, we present an innovative method that utilizes Twitter data to predict future infection rates and monitor public sentiment. We employ a novel approach known as the Generalized Mean Disclaimer for handling sentiment analysis, as well as a cutting-edge neural network called the Multi-Task Neural Model for analyzing data and making predictions. Our experiment, conducted using real world data from the WHO and Twitter, demonstrates that our model successfully anticipates future infection rates and captures the evolution of public sentiment in real time. Moreover, our findings indicate that our model's infection rate predictions are 94% accurate within a certain time frame, and can be trained with just 300 daily data points. This is a significant advancement, given that previous models required substantially larger datasets. Our code is openly accessible on GitHub at the specified URL. Advances in artificial intelligence, coupled with enhanced access to social media data, will enable similar applications in the future, leading to novel solutions for addressing public health crises. A theoretical framework is introduced to analyze the physics of layered cuprate superconductors by treating 3D structures as 2D systems with minimal 3D effects. Utilizing this approach, we re-examine the distribution of charge across the CuO$_{6}$ planes and re-classify the phases of cuprates based on intralayer and interlayer couplings, interacting electrons, and other relevant parameters. Our framework simplifies the complex patterns of charge distribution observed in cuprates, providing a more straightforward understanding of the relationships between these features and the superconducting transitions that occur within them. It also enables us to identify potential pathways for superconductivity by following the effects of variations in the coupling between layers on the distribution of charge within layers. Our analysis highlights the significance of intralayer coupling over interlayer coupling in terms of the superconducting transitions that occur within the phases of cuprates. Lastly, we discuss the implications of our framework for the fundamental physics of layer-based superconductors and discuss the requirements for developing a more comprehensive theory of superconductivity within these materials. Our study is accompanied by a revised phase diagram for cuprates, featuring a new organization of the layers based on intralayer and interlayer couplings, and we predict a new phase of cuprates, anticipated to exhibit higher critical currents than existing records. Lastly, we propose an experimental design for detecting the predicted high-current phase and discuss the potential for this experiment to reveal additional insights into the superconducting transitions within cuprates. Our framework is applicable to any layer-based superconducting structure and can be used to inform the design of experiments and the development of new theories within this field.

By comparing observations and theoretical predictions, we investigated how dust affects the cooling in the outer regions of a protoplanetary disk. Our analysis revealed that the observed microwave emission in Sgr A* cannot be accounted for by radiative energy transfer, but a significant exception exists in the case of protoplanetary disks. Additionally, a notable discrepancy exists between the predicted Extinction Curve and the observed one in the direction of Sgr A*, which cannot be reproduced by modeling the dust in the surrounding disk. This discrepancy suggests an intrinsic variation in the near-infrared spectrum of Sgr A*, which cannot be explained by radiative cooling. A possible explanation for this spectral signature could be the presence of a massive planet in the disk, its absorption indicative of a discontinuity in the disk's structure, or dust particles evaporated by the star's gravitational force. Dust composition plays a crucial role in understanding the behavior of the disk, especially when considering elements like Silicon and Oxygen, which show significant abundance variations when comparing Sgr A* with other protoplanetary disks. As a result, we propose that the absence of dust recombination in the direction of Sgr A* could be attributed to the absence of copious gas conditions in this location. Consequently, the absence of recombination emission allows for a more accurate estimation of the microwave emission temperature in this region. Ultimately, the unique features of the disk surrounding Sgr A* justify independent observational efforts to study this complex astrophysical system. The shape of the Sun's gravitational influence on nearby stars, known as the Roche lobe, affects astrometric measurements. A key effect is the variation of parallax with ecliptic latitude, impacting high-precision astrometry, particularly in the microlensing surveys of the Solar System. The complexity of this phenomenon becomes apparent when considering the shifting location of the Sun's gravitational influence as the Earth orbits the Sun. To accurately account for this effect in forthcoming surveys, a simple and efficient method of calculating the parallax shift has been developed. This method is based on approximating the gravitational potential of the Solar System using a combination of point masses, and incorporates the unique perspective of the Earth as it moves around the Sun. The model includes the effects of the Solar System's components, but focuses on the dominant influence of the Sun. The parallax shift is calculated through a series of transformations, and a set of coefficients is provided to simplify the process. This approach is relevant to the ongoing MMAS survey, and can be applied to other similar surveys with similar instrumentation and fields of view. The accuracy of this method is validated through a comparison with the results of more complex simulations. The parallax shift is found to be greatest at high ecliptic latitudes, and follows a symmetrical distribution as expected for a gravitational effect caused by the Solar System's components. The model is also applicable to the microlensing findings reported in the literature, and provides a useful tool for planning observations and analyzing data in future surveys. The implementation of this method is already underway for the forthcoming SPAS survey, and is likely to be of interest to other similar surveys as well. This study introduces novel algorithms for approximating nonlinear dynamics at a specific state and constructing low-dimensional models. The newly discovered HI clouds in our local universe are largely unknown, especially those in the Orion region. Using the VLA, we conducted a high-resolution observation of HI clouds in Orion using the hyperfine structure absorption line method. These clouds were detected at a distance of 0.7-1.7 kpc from the Galactic plane. The results show that the HI clouds in Orion have a mass of 100-5000 M, a diameter of 1-11 parsecs, and a velocity dispersion of 6-50 km/s. The position-velocity diagrams of the HI clouds in Orion reveal spiral arms and a faint outer arm. The inner arm consists of two clouds at a distance of 0.7 kpc from the Galactic plane and is moving at 15 km/s. The outer arm is a continuous cloud at a distance of 1.4 kpc from the Galactic plane and is moving at 50 km/s. The HI clouds in Orion are interacting with the nearby spiral galaxies, specifically the Pinwheel Galaxy, and are influenced by the dark matter in the Orion region. This research provides a method to study HI clouds in the local universe and offers a new perspective on the HI distribution in our galaxy. It also highlights the difficulty of modeling the HI clouds in Orion due to their complex structure and the limitations of using a static potential. However, it suggests that future observations and modeling approaches have the potential to shed more light on the formation and evolution of the HI clouds in Orion. This research also sets the stage for using the hyperfine structure absorption line method to study HI clouds in the local universe. The success of question answering systems relies on accurate knowledge representation and efficient knowledge retrieval. While existing knowledge retrieval-based question answering systems excel in simple questions, they often struggle with more complex queries that require in-depth knowledge understanding. This paper argues that such complexities arise from a mismatch between the vocabulary distribution in knowledge bases and the language used in questions, which can be mitigated through a two-pronged approach. First, a semantic-driven method is employed to select suitable knowledge candidates based on their semantic relationships. Second, a distributional perspective is used to select the most linguistically appropriate knowledge candidate among the semantically relevant ones. We demonstrate this paper's concept with the KBC-ZES system, which incorporates a novel QASystem that combines both approaches. Evaluations using the LAMA benchmark show that our approach outperforms existing state-of-the-art BERT-based knowledge retrieval methods, delivering an average improvement of 5.4% in accuracy across eight datasets. Moreover, our approach achieves comparable performance to state-of-the-art neural knowledge creation methods while retaining the simplicity of retrieval methods. Code and data for this paper are available at https://github.com/ghulam-eiman/kbc-zes-system.

Evaluating the performance of relational machine learning models in pharmacology, particularly in target prediction, is a challenge that needs addressing. A proposed evaluation framework, called TReMOR, is designed to assess the quality of predictions by comparing predicted target relationships to known interactions and contrasting them with random predictions. This framework creates a ranking of predicted relationships and incorporates metrics such as mean rank and proportion of top-rank relationships to evaluate model performance. A demonstration of TReMOR's utility shows that performance indicators like mean rank and proportion of top-rank relationships can be utilized to guide enhancements to relational machine learning models, such as proteoMPN, and demonstrate the potential of these models to contribute to the discovery of new target-drug relationships. Furthermore, the framework facilitates the comparison of different evaluation strategies and reveals aspects where more sophisticated evaluation methods, such as TReMOR, are preferable to simpler approaches, such as AUC. As a result of these investigations, prototype software that utilizes TReMOR's evaluation strategies and enables the comparison of predicted target relationships is being made available to the scientific community via an open-source platform. This software is an early version and is intended to serve as a basis for discussion and to spur further development of relational machine learning models and evaluation methodologies. A leading method for modeling complex systems that process vast amounts of distributed data uses online distributed learning algorithms. These algorithms are typically trained in isolation, but they can also be designed to work together, cooperating to minimize communication requirements and efficiently share information. We investigate a unique problem where one source sends a sequence of binary messages to a receiver, who must decide whether each message indicates a positive or negative outcome based on a binary classification task. We demonstrate that the receiver's decision rule has a optimal performance and develop a discrete random walk algorithm to approach this standard. Interestingly, we find that this standard performance can be achieved with a significantly reduced communication burden, essentially achieving the optimal standard with only one bit of communication per data point. We also explore the scalability of this approach in a scenario where there is one sender and multiple receivers. Finally, we apply this standard performance as a benchmark in a real-world scenario involving online sales data.

By analyzing local interactions in the geostrophic approximation, it was found that the energy spectrum takes the form $E(k,t) \propto (k_\theta/k_g)^{4/3} \cdot (k_g/t)^2$, which verifies the results of [3, 4] and aligns with the characteristics of robust turbulence. The turbulence itself was observed to maintain its unstable state characteristics, with no signs of approaching a stable steady state. The onset of turbulence was found to be highly dependent on the initial conditions, with variations of up to 50% in the decay rates of kinetic energy for different turbulence scenarios. It was also discovered that the energy contained in modes above the critical layer ($k<k_g$) quickly dissipates due to weak intermode interactions, with a characteristic time of $t \approx 1/k_g$. As a result, the long-term behavior of the turbulence is largely determined by modes at the critical layer and above, with weak influences from weaker modes. The robust characteristics of the turbulence also suggest that it could be an example of a universality class, with the geometry of the container defining the specific parameters of the turbulence. Our research indicates that SSL models' predictions can be enforced to conform to available labeled data by using interpolation-based mixing, effectively serving as a form of regularization. The Future Extended Range Engineering (FEX) project aims to upgrade ATLAS's Level 1 trigger by leveraging a custom-built, high-speed data processing system. Comprised of three fully digital Data Concentrators (DCs), this system will handle event data at a rate of 12.8 TB/s, achieving approximately 102.4 Tbps of throughput. With the Large Hadron Collider's upcoming upgrade, where the collision frequency will increase from 40 to 172.5 MHz, the FEX system is designed to handle up to 172.5 million 10-bit samples per second. To optimize performance and energy efficiency, the FEX system employs a three-stage design, featuring large, 10-Gbps Ethernet-connected memory banks that facilitate fast data buffering and enable the Data Concentrators to operate at the detector's native 40 MHz before further processing. A fully functional prototype of the Data Concentrator has been constructed and demonstrated. This prototype, which combines three 40-Gbps Optical Receivers, twelve 10-Gbps Optical Transceivers, fifteen 10-Gbps Ethernet connections, and a custom Digital Signal Processor, has successfully operated the FEX front-end readout interface and triggered the ATLAS detector's front-end drivers in real-time. With approximately 5.7 watts of power consumption per channel, the FEX system offers the best power-to-performance ratio for its kind, and is now undergoing integration with the ATLAS trigger system. Once integrated, the system will undergo comprehensive testing to ensure it can effectively handle various detector simulations and real data scenarios. The successful development of the FEX system will serve as a foundation for future upgrades and exploration of its applications in other particle physics experiments. The project's knowledge gained and developed components will also be made available to other projects and research areas within CERN. The FEX project is anticipated to be fully integrated into the ATLAS detector by 2023, in time for the Large Hadron Collider's High-Luminosity Upgrade. Reconstructing real-world objects and environments from video or 3D data for subsequent use in a variety of applications remains a challenging and open-ended task. To achieve this goal, researchers have developed various frameworks that learn to map images to their corresponding 3D scenes. However, these models often focus exclusively on static scenes, neglecting the movement and transformation of objects within them. To address this shortfall, the Articulated Neural Renderer uses 3D models composed of both mesh structures and kinetic graphics to model dynamic objects and their underlying physics. This novel approach builds upon previous work, combining elements of both structure-from-motion analysis and kinematic inference to accurately depict moving subjects from just a single image. Through significant enhancements to input data, including the addition of supplementary 3D information and video content, Articulated Neural Renderer exhibits substantial performance gains over existing models in various evaluation metrics. The framework's capabilities also extend beyond prediction, with uses such as optimizing scene graphics for visualization and removing background noise from moving objects. The code for Articulated Neural Renderer is now available online.

By utilizing graph neural networks to analyze local atomic configurations, researchers have been able to predict material properties accurately. Additionally, existing protocols for quantifying local atomic configurations are limited to simple descriptors like superatoms, and there's a lack of protocols that can capture complex structures. This paper addresses these shortcomings by developing new protocols to analyze local atomic configurations within crystalline structures and incorporating graph neural networks into these protocols. These protocols were effectively validated through precision and recall metrics when applied to binary III-V semiconductors and II-VI semiconductors, and they were able to accurately predict the energy gaps of these materials. We examine how a key property, surjectivity, of a second-order elliptic differential operator, $P$, affects the behavior of $P$ on smooth functions, addressing specific questions that have been debated among experts. To do this, we introduce an associated bilinear form and investigate its properties, particularly its definiteness, which is crucial for understanding the behavior of $P$ on smooth functions. Our study demonstrates that if the bilinear form's surjectivity is limited to a subset of smooth functions, it is not necessarily surjective for all smooth functions. Conversely, we prove that if $P$ is surjective on all smooth functions, its associated bilinear form's surjectivity for the same set of functions follows directly. Additionally, this implies that if $P$ is not surjective on all smooth functions, there exists a non-zero smooth function, $u$, such that its image under $P$ and the bilinear form's image under $u$ are both zero. This result further indicates that if $P$ is not surjective on all smooth functions, its failure to be surjective can be characterized through its behavior on this specific subset of smooth functions, which simplifies the characterization of this aspect of $P$'s behavior. This simplified understanding is achieved by defining a new operator, $Q$, which acts on the same domain and range as $P$, but has a similar elliptic structure, and establishing that $Q$'s failure to be surjective on all smooth functions has the same character as $P$'s failure. To do this, we establish that $Q$ is essentially equivalent to $P$ when considering their behavior on smooth functions, which is done by demonstrating that if $P$ is not surjective on all smooth functions, there exists a non-zero smooth function, $u$, such that its image under $P$ and the bilinear form's image under $u$ are both zero, which provides the desired characterization of $P$'s failure to be surjective on all smooth functions. This study is applicable to any second-order elliptic differential operator, $P$, and is therefore broadly applicable. Notably, this research is relevant to the analysis of closed, non-linear partial differential equations, which often involves understanding the properties of related operators, such as $P$. By examining these properties, researchers can gain insight into the behavior of these equations, which can be critical to establishing existence, uniqueness, and stability results for their solutions. We introduce FedBuff, an innovative framework that combines robust scaling and privacy preservation in federated learning. Speech recognition systems can be highly accurate in their native language, but perform significantly worse in languages with little similarity. This research explores the potential of transfer learning to improve performance across language barriers. We begin by applying a transfer learning approach to speech recognition, using a system pre-trained on English to recognize German sounds. This leads to a 30% reduction in training time and a 10% improvement in accuracy compared to starting from scratch. Building on this success, we further investigate the effects of transfer learning using multiple pre-trained languages. We trained speech recognition systems for five languages: English, German, Dutch, Spanish, and Czech. The models were pre-trained and fine-tuned in the order of their linguistic similarity to English. This order was determined by combining native speaker judgments with objective linguistic metrics. Our findings show that transfer learning yields consistent gains across all languages, with a 10% improvement on average. When modeling similarity to English is the primary factor, the best performance is achieved by fine-tuning the model in that order. However, when other factors are considered, the best performance is achieved by fine-tuning the model at random. Our research paves the way for further investigation into transfer learning in multi-language speech recognition systems. The code and data used in this research are available online. Precise force control in series elastic actuators is highly dependent on accurate measurement of the elastic element's force-displacement behavior. However, determining this behavior is complicated due to nonlinearities in the elastic element and sensing errors in the measurement system. Furthermore, maintaining precise force control during long-duration tasks is challenging because the elastic element's behavior degrades over time due to its own nonlinear properties and the influence of stick-slip friction. To address this issue, a method is proposed to estimate the elastic element's behavior based on data from a set of discrete measurement points, obtained by systematically varying the actuator's position while controlling the actuator's movement to follow a straight line. This method first generates a series of force readings at distinct position values, and subsequently, uses a technique called chaotic differential evolution to select the optimal combination of these data points for an elastic element model that can be analytically solved. By using this model, the actuator is capable of achieving precise force control during long-duration tasks. Experimental results confirm the efficacy of this approach. A notable benefit of this method is that it allows the actuator to maintain precise force control even when the elastic element's behavior has changed over time, without requiring any additional data. This method's ability to handle sensor errors and nonlinearities makes it suitable for a wide range of applications involving series elastic actuators. Moreover, the proposed method can be easily adapted for use in various elastic element models. Additionally, the method provides an advantageous way to integrate sensory feedback and nonlinear element behavior, and can be an useful tool for educational purposes in computer-based courses on mechanics and control systems. A demonstration program written in C is also included as a resource for readers. A potential drawback of this method is that its computational complexity can result in control decisions being made at a rate of only 10 Hz or less, which may not be sufficient for some applications requiring faster decision-making. By analyzing networks of up to 4 layers and starting with 6 or more inputs, scientists discovered that a greater number of inputs can be sorted with accuracy as networks become more multi-layered. Furthermore, this knowledge led to a re-examination of the relationship between network depth and the minimum number of inputs it can effectively sort, revealing that previously held assumptions were inaccurate. Moreover, this new understanding prompted an exploration into the specific values that sorting networks can take on with low arity and higher depths, revealing that the applicable values increase with deeper networks. Ultimately, this work has implications for the broader field of algorithmic decision making.

The effect of magnetic fields on the formation of merger remnants in gas-rich major mergers remains unclear. A comprehensive study was conducted using high-resolution simulations of merging galaxies. These simulations, based on advanced magnetohydrodynamic algorithms, accurately captured the behavior of magnetic fields in merging galaxies. The research revealed that magnetic fields in merging galaxies grow significantly due to turbulence and the accumulation of magnetic fields within magnetic islands. However, in the final stages of mergers, these fields become distorted and ultimately lost in the intense magnetic fields generated by the merging of magnetic fields in the central regions. Interestingly, the inclusion of magnetic fields in the simulations prevented the formation of massive, dense disks and effectively redirected matter towards the central regions. The central black hole experienced a substantial growth spurt as a result of the increased supply of matter. The findings also showed that magnetic fields led to the production of smaller, more numerous star clusters, which, when combined with weaker magnetic fields, resulted in larger clusters. The inclusion of magnetic fields in the simulations produced merger remnants with characteristics more akin to low-redshift galaxies, such as active nuclei and massive star clusters. The models with magnetic fields also exhibited greater nuclear gas reserves and higher rates of star formation, accompanied by larger molecular clouds in the central regions. The inclusion of magnetic fields, however, failed to improve the agreement between the models and observed spectra of merging galaxies at low redshift. The simulations with magnetic fields demonstrated distinct patterns of gas velocity and chemical abundance profiles, which could be differentiated from magnetic-free simulations and further distinguished from low-redshift galaxy data. The primary challenge in adapting Generalized Early Commitment (GEC) from traditional sequence-to-sequence transfer learning lies in identifying model components responsible for timing adjustments. While recent adaptations employ multi-task learning with closely related tasks, our proposed method instead incorporates a task-specific time-gating mechanism inspired by the Early Commitment model's timing characteristics. In our experiments, adapting GEC via this approach proves more effective than baseline multi-task transfer learning strategies, allowing for precise control over timing adjustments and generation quality. Our results demonstrate that incorporating a time-gating mechanism into adapter modules enables successful GEC adaptations even without access to labeled data, as shown by adaptations without data labeled with timing annotations. Furthermore, our analysis highlights the potential risks and benefits associated with using GEC adaptations and reveals that many adaptations exhibit similar performance to our proposed method when using unscaled weights, prompting questions about the nature of representations learned in these models. Our code is available at https://github.com/UltimaInMemory/GEC-Adapter.

In 2020, Japan faced a significant suicide crisis compounded by the COVID-19 pandemic.
In response, the Japanese government introduced a unique crisis-prevention measure: it rounded
suicide rates to the nearest five, with rates below fifteen considered low, between fifteen and
thirty considered intermediate, and above thirty considered high.
This study investigates the effect of this rounding on statistical inferences about suicide rates in
Japan from 2008 to 2020.
Given the explicit definitions of rounded rates, we model the real suicides as a mixture of three
components: low, intermediate, and high rates.
By applying the Poisson mixture model, we successfully estimated the time-dependent mixing proportions
and mean suicide rates for the three components.
Our analysis reveals that the government's rounding led to significant distortions in statistical inferences,
especially for low rates, where the estimated mean rate was substantially lower than the actual mean rate.
On the other hand, the estimated mean rate for intermediate and high rates was only slightly lower than the actual mean rate.
Furthermore, we evaluated the impact of the rounding on suite detection by applying the Sharp-School method.
Our results show that the rounding led to a decrease in the duration of periods with elevated suicide rates but had little effect on the detection of suicide peaks.
Ultimately, we stress the importance of communicating suicide rates in their original form to avoid misleading the public.

We have investigated the optical properties of GdInO3, a pyrochlore-type 4d-5t transition metal compound, by employing ab initio calculations based on the DFT. Our studies reveal that GdInO3 exhibits notable positive charge polarization and optical excitations, contradicting the conventional predictions of the random phase approximation. Additionally, our findings suggest that GdInO3 shares commonalities with 5d iridates in terms of their optical structures, and our predicted phase diagram for the GdInO3 series aligns with experimental data. Notably, our results demonstrate that exchange-coupled 4d electrons exhibit unique characteristics distinct from those of 5d electrons, with an example being the absence of a Mott-insulator state in GdInO3. This outcome is attributed to the larger spatial extension of 4d orbitals, leading to increased screening and less exchange interaction. Further, our analysis of the GdInO3 series reveals that the rise in lattice constant results in a transition from Mott-insulator to small-polaron behavior with decreasing Gd ion concentration. This transition is predicted to occur at a critical hole concentration of 0.02 per Gd ion site. Our research provides a theoretical framework for the understanding of correlated 4d electrons in 4d-5t transition metal compounds, offering novel perspectives on the fundamental properties of these complex materials. Moreover, our predicted phase diagram of the GdInO3 series is highly relevant to ongoing experimental research. Consequently, our studies are expected to pave the way for the exploration of novel materials featuring 4d-5t transition metal compounds with pyrochlore, anti-perovskite, or honeycomb lattice structures. These complex lattice configurations are anticipated to give rise to exceptional magnetic properties, such as magnetic frustration and strong coupling between magnetic ions. Ultimately, this research is expected to contribute to a deeper comprehension of the unique characteristics of 4d electrons in transition metal compounds. Lastly, our study on GdInO3 is expected to provide a foundation for a predicted trend in the phase diagram across the GdInO3 series, with further investigation required to uncover the underlying factors contributing to these outcomes. Additionally, our ab initio derived density of states has been compared with experimental photoemission data, yielding an indication of charge contents for Gd and In ions. In the context of multi-item auctions with diverse buyer groups, a separate auction is typically held for each individual item. This approach often results in inefficient allocation and significant financial losses for bidders. To address this issue, researchers have been exploring non-discriminatory pricing mechanisms that allow for fair allocation of multiple items to the same buyer. Focusing on the scenario where a single buyer has distinct values for each item, various methods have been proposed to determine a fair allocation. One such approach, proposed by Ayaydin and Devanur in their study, suggests using the round-robin mechanism to achieve this goal. Their research compares the fairness guarantees of this approach to that of the cut-and-choose algorithm. To extend this approach to multiple bidders, they introduce an alternative strategy and provide a fair allocation scheme based on the price of stability concept. This proposed method offers guaranteed fairness to a degree proportional to the degree of efficiency achieved by the strongest auction algorithm. Additionally, they investigate conditions under which this proposed method results in allocations that are nearly efficient in scenarios with limited buyer diversity. As a further contribution, they provide explicit fairness guarantees for several benchmark mechanisms, including the round-robin, cut-and-choose, and uniform-price mechanisms. This research offers a theoretical framework for determining non-discriminatory prices that ensure fair multi-item allocation to individual bidders, and also offers practical allocation strategies in various scenarios. Moreover, their studies can serve as a foundation for extending fair allocation methods to more complex scenarios.  This research is contingent on prior work established by Ayaydin and Devanur. This document delves into comparative fairness guarantees of the round-robin mechanism and cut-and-choose algorithm, and also ponders whether similar techniques could guarantee efficiency in diverse auction scenarios. Using multiple translations of the same target image can significantly enhance pseudo-labeling for target data. Unlike previous approaches that rely on selecting the most accurate translation, our research averages predictions across all translations, demonstrating this simple averaging strategy yields superior results. We support this finding with theoretical insights showing it minimizes a divergence measure between distributions. Building on this success, we incorporate averaging in a self-learning framework, dubbed CoCoXLS, and validate the benefits in pseudo-labeling through experiments on Cifar-10, Cifar-100, and Places-365 datasets, achieving improved performance compared to existing self-learning methods. We obtained high-resolution radio observations of the HII region population in UGC 8839, a spiral galaxy that resembles our own Milky Way, and analyzed the data to determine the spatial distribution of its HII regions. Unlike the spiral arms in UGC 8839, which show a distinct ring-like shape, the HII regions show a more even distribution across the galaxy disk. Compared to similar regions in other spiral galaxies, UGC 8839 has a notably larger population of HII regions located close to its center. Based on modeling, we found that the presence of a bar-shaped structure in UGC 8839 is likely the main factor contributing to this distribution, with the potential to enhance gas gas accretion onto the central disk by a factor of 5-10. Along with SBS 0710+541, UGC 8839 provides significant insight into the observed correlation between spiral arm width and central black hole mass in galaxies like our own Milky Way. Upcoming high-resolution radio observations of UGC 8839 will allow for further analysis of the galaxy's central region, which may provide additional evidence for the presence of a bar-shaped structure and shed light on its potential effects on gas dynamics in the galaxy's core.

By incorporating this strategy into a query optimization framework, we can achieve optimal performance while maintaining desirable security standards. In addition, an exploration of real-world applications highlights the potential applications of this technique in prominent databases. Understanding how machine learning models make their decisions is crucial for their widespread adoption. By focusing on a model's core constraints that are inherently unsatisfiable, we can identify the key features responsible for its predictions. We introduce a new approach to computing Minimal Unsatisfiable Cores (MUC) for Boolean constraints, building on recent improvements to Boolean constraint solving. Our algorithm leverages the same highly optimized SAT solvers used for model selection and can compute MUCs for large-scale NLP tasks. We demonstrate the effectiveness of MUC-based feature importance metrics in complex real-world scenarios. Additionally, we show that our approach provides more accurate and interpretable results for modern machine learning models, specifically in the context of tree ensembles and neural networks. We also offer an interactive tool allowing users to explore the MUC-based feature importance metrics in our repository. Experimental evaluations are conducted as part of the accompanying paper available at this link. We are also contributing our code to an ongoing competition in machine learning interpretability.

Recently, deep learning techniques have gained popularity in the automated detection and segmentation of surgical instruments within complex surgical scene images. To enhance accuracy, attention-based mechanisms and encoder-decoder networks have been combined in models such as the Dual Decoder Attention Network (DDANet). In a comparative study, DDANet demonstrated superior performance compared to other deep learning networks, including U-Net, FCN, and ResUNet. However, the analysis indicated that DDANet's segmentation output was highly reliant on accurate detection of the instrument's boundary, with limited consideration given to the instrument's interior. A major limitation of the study was the use of annotated boundary data, which is often absent in real-world image datasets. As a result, the model's generalizability to datasets with annotated scene content is questionable. This study's primary objective is to investigate the instrument segmentation scene context using the CPM-based attention mechanism in DDANet. A comprehensive analysis of contextual fusion scenarios was conducted, with evaluations based on boundary-annotated and scene-annotated datasets. The study demonstrated DDANet's capability to effectively integrate context from the CPM attention mechanism, leading to improved accuracy in surgical instrument segmentation, with results showing significant gains of +13.95 in boundary-annotated datasets and +10.58 in scene-annotated datasets. Moreover, the study explored context fusion approaches using annotated scene data, with findings indicating DDANet's sensitivity to context and implicit scene content. To facilitate replication and advancement of instrument segmentation research, the study's data and code are made publicly available. 

Keywords: Surgical instrument segmentation, attention mechanism, context fusion, encoder-decoder network, deep learning.

Deep learning techniques for Re-identification (ReID) have primarily focused on learning distinct identity features from labeled data. However, very few studies have explored unsupervised ReID methods using contrastive learning to eliminate within-identity disparities and expand ReID applications to label-free scenarios. To bridge this gap, this study leverages a contrastive learning approach to achieve outstanding unsupervised ReID results. Specifically, a graph-based contrastive learning framework is proposed to counter the limitations of a single contrastive approach mentioned in Section 1. This proposal involves constructing a label-free graph based on distributional contrasts, eliminating internal differences, and extracting cross-identity contrasts to broaden ReID applications. Comprehensive experiments conducted on six cross-benchmarks demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed GF-CAL, resulting in an average rank-1 accuracy of 26.36% and a rank-1/rank-5 percentage of 33.08%, outperforming the current state-of-the-art unsupervised ReID methods by a significant margin.
