In large grid worlds, efficient planning is crucial for autonomous agents to track down moving targets. The complexity of these environments makes it difficult to apply sophisticated reasoning methods, often requiring a sophisticated preprocessing stage to reduce the size of the state space. We introduce a novel approach that divides the grid into simpler sub-regions, using Monte Carlo planning to evaluate the effectiveness of a strategy within each one. As the targets move, the sub-regions may change, but our approach can handle these changes seamlessly. We show that our method outperforms existing solutions in simulations, and examine the benefits of different grid divisions and evasion strategies. The code is openly available and can be adapted for various target movement patterns. We also discuss potential applications and future improvements. The project is hosted on https://github.com/avrahami/pmc-py. We evaluate our method in a realistic scenario similar to that described in the paper, and posted the results at https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/https://drive.google.

An n-tuple of positive integers is considered nonstandard if at least one of its components does not belong to the standard set of natural numbers. We have developed a comprehensive framework for classifying these unique n-tuples as either standard, nontransitive, or supersingular within the context of nonstandard automata theory. This framework allows us to thoroughly explore the nonstandard n-tuples of up to four components and demonstrate the existence of infinitely many nonstandard, transitive 3-tuples. Additionally, we have identified both the smallest and the infinitely largest nonstandard, transitive 4-tuples, thereby providing a complete picture of our developed classification system. Moreover, we have established a direct connection between the prefix-stabilizing property and transitivity for nonstandard 3-tuples, which forms the foundation of our theory on transitive nonstandard automata. By incorporating all discovered knowledge, we have developed a hierarchical structure of our findings to ensure clarity and ease of understanding. This hierarchical structure is presented in a diagram following the definitions provided in the paper. We believe that our work on nonstandard automata theory will contribute positively to the development of automated reasoning systems and may also find applications in the broader field of formal language theory. We intend for this research to serve as a starting point for further exploration and improvement of our results by the scientific community. We hope that our work will be beneficial in advancing the discussion on the prefix-stabilizing property and its relationship with transitivity and suprasignaturability: a concept recently introduced by Ralph Back in his paper titled "Communicating Streaming Processes". We also wish to contribute positively to the development of highly efficient automated tools by establishing connections between logical properties and operational properties of programs, as advocated by Leslie Lamport in his paper titled "Checkifying a Multi-Purpose Protocol". We intend for this research to contribute to the ongoing debate on first-order logic versus temporal logic, as discussed in the paper titled "First Second-Order Logic" by William F. McCauley. We hope that our work will also facilitate the development of systems that can effectively deal with uncertain information in databases, as highlighted in the paper titled "Reasoning About Uncertainty" by Joseph Y. Halpern. We believe that our research can also help in the creation of systems that can learn from their experiences and adapt to new situations. We intend for this research to contribute to the development of systems that can reason about their own performance and improve it, as advocated by Per Andersen in his paper titled "Reasoning About Efficiency".

This paper presents a novel approach to improving the cycleGAN in the task of creating virtual scenic skylines. We investigated the limitations of the cycleGAN by testing alternative modifications to the generator module. Our research revealed that the cycleGAN's lack of domain translation guidance results in inaccurate results. To address this issue, we developed a modified version of the cycleGAN that incorporates adaptive instance normalization (AdaIN) layers. By incorporating AdaIN layers, we were able to incorporate a domain translation code into the generator module, significantly improving the accuracy of the generated images. Additionally, we introduced a new dataset containing virtual scenic skylines for evaluation purposes. When tested on this dataset, our proposed model demonstrated a higher accuracy rating than the original cycleGAN. This improvement can be attributed to the ability of the AdaIN layer to effectively implement domain translation guidance within the generator module. Moreover, we found that incorporating a domain translation code into the generator module results in more realistic generated images. Our research indicates that the use of AdaIN layers results in more accurate results than that of the cycleGAN, with an F-score of 0.746 as opposed to the original cycleGAN's F-score of 0.688. To facilitate further research, we are making the new dataset and accompanying code publicly available. This will enable other researchers to test and compare their approaches against our proposed model.

We introduce a new multi-modal dialog scoring model that incorporates context from multiple perspectives, counteracting the prevalent single-perspective design. Our proposed framework, unlike existing methods that typically use a unidirectional scoring approach, leverages context from both the sender and receiver perspectives. We demonstrate that this score function yields superior performance when evaluated on the Fundation Dataset. Moreover, our findings reveal that incorporating domain-specific context through a score function results in notable improvements in modeling dialog actions. We observe a notable boost in performance of approximately 11% when using the receiver-perspective context, and our results highlight the complex interplay between dialog context, intentions, and actions. Our approach also facilitates an interesting phenomenon where scoring model performance significantly exceeds that of action classification models when evaluated on Fundation actions, highlighting potential challenges in modeling dialog. We further examine challenges models face when evaluating Fundation's complex contexts, and propose future research directions for multi-modal dialog evaluation and modeling. Our code and data are available at: https://github.com/hjdw2/MDScorer.git. Our paper has been accepted for oral presentation at the 2022 Conference of the International Association for Computing Machinery on Artificial Intelligence and Robotics.

The concept of deformed halo structures revolves around fluctuating rotational states, specifically odd-spin states that can provide insight into the shape. To explore this, researchers studied rotating nuclei in fluorine and oxygen isotones using the deformed relativistic Hartree-Bogoliubov theory. By comparing calculations with experimental data, they determined that several parameters, including binding energy, separation energy, and electromagnetic transition probabilities, can serve as probes of deformed halo structures. Additionally, researchers analyzed momentum distributions within the surface region and density density correlations in rotating systems. Momentum distributions within the $1f_{5/2}$ orbit are compared to determine the influence of deformation on filling factors. The findings suggest that rotating deformed halo nuclei exhibit unique features, with densities within the $1f_{5/2}$ orbit at the surface being twice as high as in traditional halo nuclei, thus providing supporting evidence for the deformed halo model. The moment of inertia in $^{42}$Mg is investigated and found to be consistent with that of neighboring even-spin isotones, however exhibiting an anomalous increase in moment of inertia in $^{25}$O. The density density correlations in $^{42}$Mg and $^{25}$O reveal a distinct shape in rotating deformed halo nuclei, displaying enhanced correlations within the $1f_{5/2}$ orbit at the surface. This work provides a framework for a deeper understanding of rotating deformed halo nuclei and encourages experimental verification of predicted features. Theoretical predictions are made for $^{25}$O, $^{26}$O, $^{27}$O, $^{41}$Mg, and $^{42}$Mg. The study anticipates that rotation will be insufficient to destroy the deformed halo structure in these isotones. The proposed research is suggested to be carried out using reactions with relativistic or intermediate energies and electromagnetic probes, such as $\gamma$-ray spectroscopy, but could also be investigated via deep inelastic scattering or stable beam experiments. The ultimate goal of this research is to shed light on the complex relationships between rotation, deformation, and halo structures in nuclei. Recent video super-resolution models have achieved remarkable success due to the advancement of deep learning techniques, however, most of these models are lagging in real-world applications because of their inability to process high-resolution videos efficiently. To bridge this gap, we develop a new video super-resolution framework called BasicVSR++, which significantly improves upon its predecessor BasicVSR by boosting PSNR performance and enhancing computational efficiency. By incorporating an adaptive cross-domain fusion module and streamlining the residual learning process, BasicVSR++ surpasses BasicVSR in PSNR metrics while also reducing the number of parameters. Moreover, the optimized memory allocation and novel temporal smoothness module in BasicVSR++ result in elevated performance and computational efficiency, making it an exceptional video super-resolution model. The source code of BasicVSR++ is publicly available at https://github.com/zeangco/BasicVSR++, where our benchmark experiments can also be found. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach achieves superior performance (around 0.53 dB) and elevated efficiency (around 0.79) when compared to the renowned VSR benchmark. Moreover, our model succeeds in boosting PSNR metrics (around 0.20 dB) and elevating computational efficiency (around 0.91) when pased through a pruned network, thereby highlighting its versatility. The benchmark experiments and code are publicly available at https://github.com/zeangco/BasicVSR++. The evolution in question occurs through the interplay between perturbative QCD, electroweak interactions, and the behavior of PDFs at low parton energies as outlined in our work on arXiv:1805.02599, with the corresponding evolution equations for PDFs now solved numerically for a broader range of parton energies. The updated PDFs are referred to as NNPDF30-nS and are comparable to the ABMP16 ABM PDFs at higher energy scales, with the ABM PDFs exhibiting a breakdown in the face of universal corrections as energy scales increase beyond $\Log(10^3)$. Despite the significant potential of model-based reinforcement learning, a major limitation of using a single learned dynamics model is the increased risk of model bias. This limitation is particularly pronounced in multi-task reinforcement learning applications. A more robust approach involves using a set of models, with each model responsible for a specific task. However, this method is often impractical due to the high cost of training multiple models in complex domains. In our research, we explore a more feasible alternative: using a set of models with varying levels of accuracy, learned through a training process that optimizes a trade-off between performance and a proxy measure of predictive error. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach in multi-task reinforcement learning, using a scenario that combines the training of models for different start states in a complex gridworld environment. Our results show that this method allows for the isolation of optimal policies for specific start states, without compromising the performance on other states. Notably, we found that this method successfully avoided the negative side effects often experienced in single-model learning, such as policy interference. We further highlight the key aspects of our approach, including the benefits of using a model hierarchy, and provide insights into the implications of our research for the broader field of model-based reinforcement learning. Generalized balanced sampling (GBS) is an advanced technique used to select a representative random sample from a larger population. The standard algorithm for GBS, devised by Devry and Deville, sustains the balance constraint at each selection stage, choosing the next sample based on the existing balance structure. A newly developed exponential-time algorithm addresses this limitation by ensuring the maximum balance at each step, thus enhancing the selection of diverse and dispersed samples. Although the exponential-time algorithm yields optimal results, its computational expense is too high for large populations. The proposed hybrid algorithm, a combination of the two methods, leverages the strengths of both approaches. It employs the exponential-time algorithm for initial balanced sampling and switches to the standard method for subsequent selections, given that the sub-samples remain relatively balanced. The hybrid algorithm's performance was evaluated on populations of varying sizes and characterized by complex balance structures. The results show that the hybrid algorithm achieves near-optimal efficiency, especially for smaller initial sample sizes, and significantly outperforms the standard algorithm, especially in the context of medical research, such as stratified randomized sampling. The hybrid algorithm is an important advancement, making generalized balanced sampling more feasible and efficient for a broader range of applications. A deep neural network is introduced in this paper for speech signal generation, based on a cascaded framework that divides the signal into multiple frequency bands. Each band has a dedicated model that learns from both the previous band in the cascade and the speech spectrum, enabling the capture of quasi-periodic patterns. In contrast to prior approaches, the cascaded structure is achieved without feeding the entire previous output as input. Instead, only the predicted spectral values and residual signals from preceding bands are utilized as input, which simplifies the network and prevents information from previous bands from being muddled together. Moreover, a novel training technique is proposed where the error from each band's prediction is fed back to the corresponding band, which speeds up convergence. Our model outperforms the baseline WaveNet model both subjectively and objectively, with results showing superior quality and consistency. Additionally, the cascaded structure was found to offer a 50% reduction in parameter count without compromise on performance. To further validate our approach, a comparison with alternative architectures including a cascaded LSTM model and a simple spectral transformer model was conducted, which revealed the efficacy of our proposed method. This study examines how the composition of gases like CO, CO2, and NH3 vary in temperate planets situated within their host star's habitable zones. We conducted a comprehensive analysis that accounts for atmospheric particles and gases at multiple wavelength lengths. Our research indicates that although the composition of these gases appears irregular at first glance, there's actually a consistent pattern. When considering multiple possible systems, we identified the most plausible configurations and calculated the resulting abundance of these gases. We discovered that CO and CO2 exhibit similar patterns, and their abundance is significantly influenced by the system's metal content, while NH3 abundance is largely unaffected. We also found that CO and CO2 abundance are directly linked to each other, and NH3 follows a distinct pathway. We created 2D and 3D plots to visualize these relationships and the impact of system metal content and habitable zone width on gas abundance. These findings provide a foundation for understanding how atmospheric compositions evolve over time and could be used to reverse engineer existing exoplanet atmospheres. Additionally, this research may help identify biomarkers for life detection in exoplanet atmospheres and inform strategies for observing these planets. Lastly, this study may also contribute to a deeper comprehension of how exoplanet atmospheres form and evolve, shaping our view of these planets and their potential for hosting life. We introduce VGG-Sound Source (VGG-SS), a comprehensive benchmark consisting of 80,000 annotated sound sources, along with source code and a listener evaluation platform. VGG-SS surpasses previous datasets with its large size, diverse sources, and detailed annotations, featuring 13 categories of forms, locations, movements, textures, and voices. To create this benchmark, we developed a pioneering listening-based approach that learns from multiple sources and outperform existing sound source recognition methods, demonstrating state-of-the-art performance on the newly created VGG-SS dataset. Comprehensive evaluations using different models and data scenarios showcase the capability of this approach, along with a unique insight into source code efficiency. Moreover, human evaluations of our listening-based models reveal surprising yet compelling results, highlighting potential future research directions. The source code, annotation guidelines, and data are available at https://github.com/vggscapes/VGG_SoundSource. The dataset can be accessed via the VGG-Sound Source dataset page. Human evaluation results are included in the appendix available at https://vggscapes.github.io/evaluations/.

Recently, graph convolutional networks (GCNs) have gained popularity for tackling graph classification tasks. Researchers have extended GCNs to operate within hyperbolic space, taking advantage of its capability to represent trees and planar graphs using a single point. We develop the Lorentzian graph convolutional network (LGCN), a new model that leverages the power of the Lorentzian space to enhance hyperbolic GCN performance. By introducing a learned point in the Lorentzian space, LGCN learns node features that can differ from those of hyperbolic GCNs, leading to better representation accuracy as measured by correlation. Furthermore, LGCN achieves higher classification accuracy than hyperbolic GCNs on datasets featuring tree structures and complex graphs, such as NCI1 and Mutag. Additionally, LGCN is more computationally efficient than hyperbolic GCNs in terms of training time. We also explore the influence of the learned point on Lorentzian space and provide insights into its potential applications. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/cyfan2015/LGCN. This study focuses on enhancing stability in the solution of an inverse problem for an acoustic partial differential equation (PDE). Specifically, it investigates the observable operator property within the boundary measurement data. Theoretical stability estimates are obtained for both smooth and non-smooth domains, with the latter involving a uniqueness proof for a related ill-posed problem. These results leverage the concept of observability inequalities, which are demonstrated to hold globally in smooth domains or locally in non-smooth domains, implying that a singular value decomposition of the operator can be obtained. Consequently, this leads to a decay rate in the conditional stability estimate, which is critical for regularizing ill-posed problems. The study also addresses the issue of reconstructing a non-smooth obstacle by establishing a uniqueness proof for a related inverse problem with data completeness. This uniqueness result ensures that an explicit reconstruction method exists, which can be used to recover information about the singular values and the shape of the non-smooth obstacle. The results obtained enhance previous studies, providing stronger stability and uniqueness results that are critical for developing practical reconstruction methods. Theoretical stability estimates are verified through numerical experiments with a finite element implementation. The explicit reconstruction approach is validated through additional numerical experiments, demonstrating its applicability to recovering non-smooth obstacles. The material is relevant to the research of challenging inverse problems, such as reconstructing complex geological structures or detecting small soft obstacles. The approach developed here is expected to inspire further investigation into the role of observability inequalities in the analysis of the operator and its implications for the conditional stability of the solution. The study is also motivated by the need to overcome difficulties in solving the direct problem numerically, particularly in non-smooth domains, and the limitations of current reconstruction methods, which often rely on unrealistic assumptions about the support of the obstacle. The results provide a foundation for developing more effective numerical solutions and better understanding the fundamental properties of the operator, which is critical for the success of such methods. The research is an initial step in exploring new approaches to solving an old problem and is intended to stimulate further investigation into the role of observability inequalities, the properties of the operator, and the development of more effective numerical solutions. The study is also expected to contribute to a deeper understanding of the complex relationships between geophysical measurements, the acoustic wave equation, and the structure of the Earth's interior, as well as the interactions between wave propagation, scattering, and the geometry of the obstacle, which are fundamental to inverse problems in geophysical imaging. The results obtained are anticipated to have implications for other inverse problems involving partial differential equations

We've developed a integrated photonic device that combines an optomechanical resonator with a nearby quantum well, allowing us to observe the transmission spectrum shift (TSS) and create a map of the transmission probability at quantum states. Using finite difference methods, we analyzed the device, consisting of a photonic resonator connected to a quantum well by a narrow channel, and found that the TSS can be displayed through mechanical resonance in the photonic resonator. Furthermore, our study demonstrates that by modifying the width of the channel, we can control the transmission probability across the quantum well, effectively opening and closing a channel for energy transmission. This effect is illustrated through a map of the transmission probability at different quantum states and we suggest it could be applied in energy transmission management. Additionally, our findings show that the optomechanical interaction strength can be adjusted through mechanical resonance in the photonic resonator, which would enable us to control the transmission probability. Consequently, this could lead to efficient transmission of energy in devices based on quantum wells. Our analysis also identifies potential sources of decoherence, specifically mechanical loss in the photonic resonator and the quantum well, although we note that these mechanisms could be minimized through advanced fabrication techniques. Nevertheless, our research provides a foundation for exploring other integrated quantum devices based on optomechanical interactions. Finally, we propose using this TSS effect to develop a quantum meter that could measure the quantum states of distant quantum wells by monitoring the TSS in the photonic resonator. This could have significant implications for the development of integrated quantum sensors and meters. Ultimately, our study offers a framework for analyzing integrated quantum devices based on optomechanical interactions and suggests potential applications for these systems. We examine the Tsallis distribution through the lens of self-organizing systems, exploring how it can arise from fundamental dynamics of preference reinforcement. By applying the principles of statistical physics to a general scenario of social interaction, we derive the Tsallis distribution as a specific case of a broader Boltzmann distribution. We then provide a specific example of how the Tsallis distribution can emerge in a coalition formation game. Our aim is to provide a theoretical framework that demonstrates the ubiquity of the Tsallis distribution in social systems, and to suggest it as a hallmark of complex social dynamics. Alongside, we discuss implications and potential empirical studies to validate our framework. We also explore connections to other distributions, such as the power law, and discuss the role of noise and adaptation in social phenomena. Furthermore, we outline opportunities for further research on social physics. Our work is a foundation for a new field of social physics that aims to uncover the universal principles governing human and animal societies by applying quantitative methods and theoretical physics. We illustrate our approach by analyzing coalitions in soccer teams and exploring the Tsallis distribution in economic systems. Ultimately, we contend that a deep understanding of social dynamics through the lens of physical laws is essential for addressing the most pressing challenges facing our world. We investigate the consequences of introducing a mass term in the perturbations of gravitational waves within a linearized gravity theory, specifically in the context of an expanding universe. Employing a conformally flat gauge seems to lead to a theory with an undesirable feature - the number of degrees of freedom increases rather than remains constant, resulting in five rather than two propagating modes. We demonstrate that this undesirable outcome is a result of selecting an inappropriate gauge, and that the true degrees of freedom remain independent of the gauge chosen. We select the kinematical gauge for our analysis, and determine the propagating modes in this gauge for both scalar and tensor perturbations. The influence of an expanding universe on the propagating modes is then computed, yielding mode frequencies directly proportional to the square root of the Hubble constant during both the matter-dominated and inflationary epochs. We further establish that the mass term can be viewed as a parameterizable Lagrangian, and incorporate the related pseudo-dynamic term into the equation of state. The resulting equation of state may be expressed as $\frac{\frac{1}{3}M^2}{H^2} + \frac{4}{3}$, and is proportional to the square of the mass term over the square of the Hubble constant, further indicating that second-order gravitational wave perturbations may provide a possible basis for addressing the $N$-problem associated with multiscalar theories of gravity. Lastly, we examine the linearized gravity theory within an expanding universe, and determine that the mass term has an undesirable effect of increasing the number of scalar degrees of freedom, resulting in a theory with an unstable behavior. Nonetheless, we are able to demonstrate that the undesirable feature is a result of selecting an inappropriate gauge, and that the true degrees of freedom remain independent of the gauge chosen. The associated instabilities in the kinematical gauge are attributed to the failure of the conformal gauge due to the expansion of the universe, resulting in the violation of the non-dynamical constraint for the scalar component, which in turn leads to the generation of an extra degree of freedom. We propose the introduction of a mass term of the Bardeen gauge to address the $N$-problem associated with multiscalar theories of gravity, and anticipate that the successful application of this approach to other theories will lead to the development of new approaches to addressing the $N$-problem. Building on a previous notion of extended double covers introduced by the second and third authors, we expand upon this concept by incorporating negative weights in a specific framework. This framework involves mapping signed graphs to planar graphs, specifically focusing on a subclass known as extended double covers. Notably, we offer three universal protocols for modeling this mapping as a pebble game, with applications to testing conic completeness and the certification of fractional chromatic numbers. Furthermore, we propose a conjecture that implies planar-completeness for a specific problem within this framework, supported by a proof of a weaker conjecture that demonstrates computational hardness for a subclass of problem instances. Additionally, we derive results for specific graph classes, including proofs of planar-completeness and the application of our frameworks to testing conic completeness. Finally, we explore the relationship between our game-theoretic approach and existing proofs of planar-completeness. This work has implications for our understanding of the chromatic number in signed graphs and may inform future research on extended double covers. It is also relevant to the study of signed graph homomorphisms and the analysis of fractional graph properties within specific classes. This work has been previously presented at mathematical conferences, and it is now being shared as a more comprehensive report.

Hybrid approximations of quantum equilibrium states can be developed using classical Hamiltonian dynamics, which is supported for four types: forward, backward, forward-backward, and tempered dynamics. This work focuses on the construction of finite-time hybrid approximations and their analysis, establishing that they can be viewed as successive applications of classical Hamiltonian dynamics and state extrapolation. Specifically, we show that such schemes can be seen as combining two basic methods: one-step Hamiltonian integration, which generates near-equilibrium states, and far-from-equilibrium state extrapolation, which allows the classical system to evolve over time. Notably, we demonstrate that the performance of these hybrid extrapolation algorithms is equivalent to utilizing classical Hamiltonian dynamics for finite periods of time. Moreover, we prove that if the one-step Hamiltonian integration is accurate, so is the finite-time hybrid approximation. We also develop a strategy for optimizing approximation parameters and provide explicit conditions for ensuring the validity of these approximations. Additionally, we demonstrate the practical efficacy of these hybrid extrapolation algorithms through concrete applications and simulations. 

Finally, we outline a potential direction for enhancing the precision of these methods by incorporating quantum extrapolation. The classical equivalents of quantum extrapolation methods are scrutinized, and their implications for quantum Hamiltonian systems are considered. The study ends with an invitation to quantum community to contribute with new ideas on this topic. 

This work is a product of collaborative efforts between the quantum community and our classical propagator development team. We believe that further collaboration will lead to more advanced classical approximations being developed, potentially surpassing the current theoretical limits.

A new deep learning network has been developed for automatically classifying and grading colorectal adenomas based on upper endoscopy video footage. This new approach, combined with a data set called HC103, marks the first time a deep learning network has been trained and tested for adenoma detection while viewing real video footage. The data set, containing 103 short video clips, was obtained from regular upper endoscopy procedures in nine different areas of the body, involving two different endoscopists. One expert provided written comments and a risk assessment for each lesion found, while another expert verified the findings and provided comments. The new network, designed to process video frames, was compared to a established network using the HC103 data set, and demonstrated enhanced accuracy of 0.845 versus 0.793 for lesion detection, and 0.677 versus 0.585 for adenoma classification, respectively. Furthermore, when tested with video footage, the new network achieved a high correlation with expert opinions of 0.772, and accurately identified adenomas in 0.677 cases. These results suggest that this new network may serve as a reliable reference standard for validating and evaluating adenoma detection systems. However, more data and diverse lesion types are still needed to further improve the network's performance. Additionally, there is a concern about the bias present in the HC103 data set, which may limit the network's effectiveness for other populations. Although the network showed potential for monitoring changes in lesions over time, more research is required to ensure its accuracy. The code for this new network has been made available online, and it is hoped that it will contribute to the development and evaluation of adenoma detection systems. Unlike conventional methods that use fixed or uniformly spaced time steps, the new time-step strategy can be adapted to model complex phenomena, such as different frequency components in a given problem. Additionally, the cost of computing each time step is factored into the optimization process, enabling the minimization of total computational costs while maintaining precise results. The success of the new method is demonstrated through numerical examples applied to difficult high-frequency acoustic scattering scenarios. Building from the parent XXZ model, we create an integrable higher-spin XXZ chain in the spin-1/2 representation. Our analysis focuses on the algebraic structure of the model, specifically the symmetry associated with the U_q(sl_2) algebra. We derive explicit expressions for the eigenvalues of the conserved charges and the diagonalized operators at the critical point (α = π/3). Furthermore, we establish a basis for the eigenstates and develop expressions for the scalar products and form factors of the primary excitations. These mathematical achievements provide a robust framework for investigating the thermodynamic properties and interacting behavior of the model. As a preliminary study, we examine the structure factors and form factors for the zero-magnetization sector. Our findings offer a foundational understanding of the spin structure factors and form factors, revealing patterns that can be exploited to analyze the thermodynamic properties. Additionally, we demonstrate that the structure factors and form factors can be computed through a combination of the algebraic Bethe ansatz and string-based ansatz for the zero-magnetization sector. Our results serve as a critical step for investigating the interacting behavior of the higher-spin XXZ chain. To further facilitate research, we are making publicly available a computational tool that enables the computation of structure factors and form factors for the zero-magnetization sector. This code can be accessed through a user-friendly web interface listed in the references. By leveraging this code and its future enhancements, we can better explore the properties of the higher-spin XXZ chain. Despite these advancements, several open questions remain, including the characterization of string solutions and the computation of structure factors and form factors for the finite-magnetization sector. These unresolved issues present significant challenges for the algebraic bethe ansatz and other analytical approaches. As such, further development of computational tools will be crucial for advancing our understanding of the higher-spin XXZ chain. Ultimately, a combination of analytical and computational methodologies will be essential for unlocking a deeper knowledge of the model's behavior.

Speech-to-text technology has made significant progress in recent years, but a major limitation remains: it nearly always requires a large amount of labeled data to function properly. This problem becomes even more challenging in situations where new domains or topics need to be covered. In our research, we focus on overcoming this obstacle through the use of zero-shot learning techniques. To build connections between the sounds of a source language and the written text of a target language, we're experimenting with two innovative methods that leverage the power of contrastive learning to build more generalizable models. Our experiments show that these models perform better in situations with only a small amount of labeled data, and they cover a wide range of languages, including ones that have very limited amounts of labeled data available. The results show that both methods are effective, but they work in different ways and have different strengths – one of them performs particularly well when the source and target languages are similar, while the other does better when they're more different.
